{
  "lesson_key": "tac-1-hello-agentic-coding",
  "title": "Hello Agentic Coding",
  "course": "TAC",
  "order": 1,
  "lesson_url": "https://agenticengineer.com/tactical-agentic-coding/course/hello-agentic-coding",
  "video": {
    "file": "tac-1-hello-agentic-coding/video/tac-1-hello-agentic-coding.mp4",
    "duration_seconds": 1311,
    "duration_display": "21:51"
  },
  "tactic": {
    "name": "Stop Coding",
    "one_liner": "Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code — hand the typing to agents and move your engineering cycles up the stack.",
    "why_uncomfortable": "It asks career engineers to retire the skill that defined them. Dan spent over a decade at startups and large companies typing code by hand — mastering languages, syntax, algorithms, data structures — and says he misses it too. The tactic demands you trust that language models running in agentic loops on supercomputers are now vastly superior coders, and that clinging to hand-typing means you have no chance of keeping up. Evolution forces us to leave skills behind to adopt new ones."
  },
  "mission": "Transform you into an engineer they can't replace — 'they' being your boss, the company, the industry, and AI itself. In a world where code is a commodity and your grandma or little brother can build an app with one prompt, you become irreplaceable the way engineers always have in technological revolutions: move up the stack. Become a commander of compute that builds systems that build systems, until your codebase runs itself.",
  "phase_model": {
    "phase1_ai_coding": "The generative-AI age's first phase: prompt-to-generate-code. Birth of vibe coders and the complete commoditization of code. You interact with the big three — context, model, prompt — to build faster than ever. Still foundational, no longer differentiating.",
    "phase2_agentic_coding": "Where real engineers strike back. A superset of AI coding: the big three plus tools — prompts that reliably execute long chains of tool calls inside an agentic coding tool. Engineers reallocate their cycles to planning, reviewing, and creating closed-loop structures, and turn their codebases into increasingly self-operating machines."
  },
  "core_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "agentic-engineer",
      "name": "The Agentic Engineer — a new role",
      "plain_english": "A software engineer whose job is not writing code but building systems that can take actions the way an engineer would: branch, write, run, test, commit, report. Dan bought agenticengineer.com in 2023 betting this role would emerge; lesson 1 declares it now exists.",
      "dan_words": "\"Predicting that a new role of software engineering would emerge, defined by the ability to build systems that can take actions as we can. It's become clear this new role now exists.\"",
      "misconception": "That 'agentic engineer' is a rebrand of 'prompt engineer.' It isn't: the role is defined by system-building (embedding agents across the SDLC), not by writing clever one-off prompts."
    },
    {
      "id": "phase-one-vs-phase-two",
      "name": "Phase 1 (AI coding) vs Phase 2 (agentic coding)",
      "plain_english": "Phase 1 = using AI to generate code faster (context, model, prompt). Phase 2 = using AI to perform engineering work end-to-end (add tools). The lesson's entire arc is the delta between these two phases, demonstrated with two prompts in one README.",
      "dan_words": "\"In the generative AI age, AI coding was phase one. Here we saw the birth of VibeCoders and the complete commoditization of code... Agentic coding marks phase two. This is where real engineers strike back.\"",
      "misconception": "That phase 2 replaces phase 1 knowledge. Agentic coding is a superset of AI coding — the big three are still there, always, even when you can't see them."
    },
    {
      "id": "stop-coding",
      "name": "Tactic #1: Stop Coding",
      "plain_english": "Stop typing code by hand. Not stop shipping code, not stop reading code — stop being the instrument that types it. Use the best tool for the job: agentic loops running powerful language models. Throughout all of TAC, not a single line of code is typed by hand.",
      "dan_words": "\"Let's end the debate right now. Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code, full stop.\"",
      "misconception": "Two opposite failure readings: (1) 'so we don't generate code anymore' — wrong, code is still a primary asset and you'll generate more than ever; (2) 'so I can stop understanding code' — wrong, code understanding is still critically important. What ends is hand-typing, and what replaces it is planning, reviewing, and closed-loop structures."
    },
    {
      "id": "commander-of-compute",
      "name": "Commander of Compute",
      "plain_english": "The identity shift of phase 2: your job is deciding where compute gets aimed and what systems it builds, not producing keystrokes. You don't just prompt to generate code — you direct compute to build systems that build systems.",
      "dan_words": "\"We move up the stack once again. We become a commander of compute... You take this compute and you use it to build systems that build systems.\"",
      "misconception": "That commanding compute means firing off more prompts manually. The command is structural — triggers, scripts, workflows that fire agents at the right time — not a human clicking faster."
    },
    {
      "id": "big-three",
      "name": "The Big Three (context, model, prompt)",
      "plain_english": "The three primitives of phase-1 AI coding: what the model can see (context), which model does the work (model), and what you ask for (prompt). Every AI coding interaction is governed by these whether you notice or not.",
      "dan_words": "\"With AI coding, you've been interacting with the big three: context, model, prompt. This is a principle of AI coding. It's always there even if you can't see it.\"",
      "misconception": "That the big three become obsolete in phase 2. They remain the foundation; phase 2 adds exactly one new dimension on top."
    },
    {
      "id": "core-four",
      "name": "The Core Four (context, model, prompt, tools)",
      "plain_english": "Add tools to the big three and you get the core four — the primitives of agentic coding. The 'tools' element specifically means prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tool calls, not the mere existence of tool calling.",
      "dan_words": "\"The new element that transforms the big three of AI coding to Agentic Coding is prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tools. When you add tools, we upgrade the big three to the core four.\"",
      "misconception": "'Tool calling has been around for a while, this is not new.' Dan's rebuttal: you're 100% right — and it's not a question of new, it's a question of scale and performance. Reliable long-chain execution is what changed."
    },
    {
      "id": "agentic-prompt",
      "name": "The Agentic (Coding) Prompt",
      "plain_english": "A prompt that contains a sequence of tool calls — a workflow specification, not a text request. It reads like a runbook (RUN / CREATE / RUN / REPORT) and executes like one: branch, write files, run programs, commit, report. It is the unit of engineering work in TAC, and every later lesson scales it.",
      "dan_words": "\"Everything we do in TAC is built upon this core idea you can see right in this readme with just 35 lines... A prompt contains a sequence of tool calls.\"",
      "misconception": "That it's 'just a prompt' — everyone knows prompts can call tools now. People don't invest the time to understand what this means at scale: fired repeatedly, with the right triggers and leverage, one prompt becomes an end-to-end developer workflow running minutes to hours without you."
    },
    {
      "id": "claude-code-form-factor",
      "name": "Claude Code's three essential elements",
      "plain_english": "Claude Code is the first agentic coding tool to properly combine: (1) a powerful language model that can reason when needed, (2) the ability to consistently call long chains of tools, and (3) the right agent architecture. That combination — being copied by every other tool — unlocks the core four, which unlocks the agentic prompt.",
      "dan_words": "\"Claude Code is the first Agentic Coding tool to properly combine three essential elements: a powerful language model that can reason when needed, the ability to consistently call long chains of tools, and the right agent architecture... Reliable Agentic Coding at scale was not possible before Claude Code.\"",
      "misconception": "That the lesson is Claude Code marketing and expires with the tool. Dan pre-handles this: your UI may differ, your models will be newer — great. The tactics are transferable to any tool with the right capabilities; don't get stuck on any one tool."
    },
    {
      "id": "programmable-agentic-coding",
      "name": "Programmable agentic coding (claude -p)",
      "plain_english": "Because Claude Code runs in the terminal, any language with terminal access can invoke it as a function: read a prompt file, pass it to `claude -p`, capture the output. The repo shows the identical pattern in shell, TypeScript+Bun, and Python+UV. The agent stops being a chat window and becomes a component you embed anywhere in the software development lifecycle.",
      "dan_words": "\"Claude Code is also a programmable Agentic Coding tool... we can run it from any programming language that has terminal access... we can embed our own agents, our own workflows, our own agentic prompts across the software development lifecycle.\"",
      "misconception": "That the demo scripts are trivial wrappers not worth running ('I already watched Dan do it'). The scripts ARE the lesson: it's not just about the agentic prompt, it's about where you can use it — including full agentic environments where you're not even present."
    },
    {
      "id": "systems-that-build-systems",
      "name": "Systems that build systems / self-operating codebase",
      "plain_english": "The end-state: codebases that increasingly run themselves — agents firing at the right time, doing the right work, with and without your oversight. Lesson 1 plants the seed (a scripted agent that does a full branch-write-run-commit-report cycle); the rest of TAC scales it.",
      "dan_words": "\"The irreplaceable engineer in phase two that we're aiming to become is the engineer that transforms their code bases into self-operating machines... so much so that your code base literally runs itself.\"",
      "misconception": "That this is hype about full autonomy tomorrow. The lesson's actual claim is incremental: 'increasingly self-operating,' built by investing your time in the right places and repeatedly extracting value."
    },
    {
      "id": "engineer-not-coder",
      "name": "You're an engineer, not a coder",
      "plain_english": "Engineering was never about writing code; it's about building systems of leverage that produce valuable outcomes for users and customers. Code is one asset those systems produce. This reframe is what makes 'stop coding' coherent rather than self-destructive.",
      "dan_words": "\"Engineering was never about writing code. It's about building systems of leverage that produce valuable outcomes for your users and your customers... Remember, you're an engineer, not a coder. The difference is massive.\"",
      "misconception": "That leverage means working more hours with AI. The 10x engineer emerges from 10x leverage, not 10x time or effort — and the number is arbitrary (2x, 10x, 100x) depending on the leverage points you find."
    },
    {
      "id": "replace-yourself",
      "name": "To become irreplaceable, replace yourself",
      "plain_english": "The lesson's closing paradox: the engineer who systematically automates their own work (replaces themselves) becomes the one the org can't replace — because they're the one who builds and commands the automation. Vibe coders can't replicate this.",
      "dan_words": "\"The contradicting truth about what you'll learn in tactical agentic coding is this: To become an irreplaceable engineer, you will replace yourself.\"",
      "misconception": "Reading it as job-loss fatalism. It's the opposite — an asymmetric-advantage strategy: in the tech industry, all the alpha lies in the future, in pushing what's possible forward."
    }
  ],
  "core_four": {
    "context": "Everything the model can see while it works: the repo, files, README instructions, settings. tac-1 keeps context deliberately tiny — one file and two directories — so the difference between the two prompts is unmissable.",
    "model": "The language model doing the work, able to reason when needed. Course-era Claude models power Claude Code; Dan explicitly blesses newer models: tools will change and models will improve — don't let that distract you.",
    "prompt": "The instruction. In phase 2 the prompt graduates from 'generate this code' to a workflow specification: the README's agentic prompt reads RUN / CREATE / RUN — a runbook, not a request for text.",
    "tools": "The fourth element and the entire phase-2 delta: file writes, terminal commands, git operations, web search — executed reliably in long chains. In tac-1 the exact tool surface is visible in .claude/settings.json: Read, Write, Edit, Bash(uv run:*), Bash(git checkout/branch/add/commit:*), WebSearch.",
    "why_scale_matters": "Dan pre-empts the obvious objection — tool calling isn't new — with: it's not a question of new, it's a question of scale and performance. Wrap the core four in the right agent architecture and prompts become long-running end-to-end AI developer workflows (minutes to hours, with and without your oversight, highly performant and self-validating), fired over and over with the right triggers at the right time. Reliable agentic coding at scale was not possible before Claude Code."
  },
  "ai_vs_agentic": {
    "ai_coding_prompt_summary": "README 'AI Coding Prompt': CREATE main_aic.py that prints 'goodbye ai coding'. One file-generation request; Claude Code writes one file with one print. Dan: 'You've seen this a million times already... This is nothing new. This is AI coding.' It represents phase 1 — code generation, even at scale.",
    "agentic_coding_prompt_summary": "README 'Agentic Coding Prompt': RUN — checkout a new/existing 'demo-agentic-coding' git branch; CREATE main_tac.py — print 'hello agentic coding' plus a concise definition of AI agents; RUN — uv run main_aic.py, uv run main_tac.py, git add ., git commit -m 'Demo agentic coding capabilities'. Claude Code plans it as a todo checklist, executes step by step by step, cleans up the todos, and reports what was done.",
    "difference_that_matters": "Both are 'just prompts,' but the second performs engineering work — branching, executing programs, committing, reporting — not just producing code. The delta is exactly one dimension (tools, reliably chained), which upgrades the big three to the core four and turns a prompt into a repeatable unit of engineering work. Dan: 'the difference between these two prompts is monumental. It's absolutely massive.'",
    "codebase_paths": [
      "README.md",
      ".claude/settings.json"
    ]
  },
  "programmable_agent": {
    "why_it_matters": "Claude Code runs in the terminal, so any language with terminal access can invoke it: read prompt.md, pass it to `claude -p`, capture output. The agent becomes a callable function — the primitive needed to embed agents, workflows, and agentic prompts across the software development lifecycle, across developer environments, including full agentic environments where you're not present (agentic triggers come later in the course). 203	  "quotes": [
204	    { "text": "You'll witness something most engineers dismiss as impossible: a codebase that nearly runs itself.", "approx_timestamp": "0:28" },
205	    { "text": "We'll understand a critical moment in the future where human in the loop review becomes a bottleneck, not a safety net.", "approx_timestamp": "2:06" },
206	    { "text": "We're operating out the loop so we can scale our impact as easily as copying a file.", "approx_timestamp": "3:17" },
207	    { "text": "This is absurd levels of scale.", "approx_timestamp": "7:08" },
208	    { "text": "The ADW directory is a scripting layer that lets us construct pipelines of agents that solve specific classes of problems back to back to back.", "approx_timestamp": "9:18" },
209	    { "text": "This isn't black and white. It's not in loop versus out loop. It's in loop moving toward out loop.", "approx_timestamp": "9:40" },
210	    { "text": "I don't care how you scale up your agent environments, it only matters that you can.", "approx_timestamp": "11:40" },
211	    { "text": "We're not solving the problem directly anymore... the rate in which you can solve your specific problem can now be drastically scaled up when you put your effort into your agentic layer.", "approx_timestamp": "13:49" },
212	    { "text": "This truly frees your agent to do one thing extraordinarily well with all the context it needs, and it lets you jump in and replay what that agent has done.", "approx_timestamp": "15:01" },
213	    { "text": "You can encode any information dense keyword that you want. You just have to make sure that your prompts recognize it and pick it up.", "approx_timestamp": "16:04" },
214	    { "text": "Remember what the review step answers. It's not 'does it work?' It's 'is what we built what we asked for?'", "approx_timestamp": "21:40" },
215	    { "text": "Teach your agent how to do it once and then run it over and over and over again and scale it across your team.", "approx_timestamp": "24:48" },
216	    { "text": "You can't vibe code this stuff. Your agent is operating as you would. You've templated your engineering.", "approx_timestamp": "27:59" },
217	    { "text": "When the agents arrived, something changed. We weren't just AI coding anymore. We started orchestrating intelligence.", "approx_timestamp": "29:21" },
218	    { "text": "This human in the loop model is a bottleneck. I'm not catching any bugs anymore. I'm not adding any value outside of the agentic layer. I'm going to remove the human in the loop review process for this class of problems.", "approx_timestamp": "30:45" },
219	    { "text": "You'll drop yourself off the end of the Outloop PITER framework and it becomes PITE, not PITER. You'll drop off the review.", "approx_timestamp": "31:19" },
220	    { "text": "This is YOLO mode for your AI developer workflows... It's maximum confidence mode for agentic engineering. No review. Just like you've stopped coding, you'll stop reviewing.", "approx_timestamp": "31:33" },
221	    { "text": "This is the lesson seven tactic: Target zero touch engineering. This is the ultimate agentic coding North Star.", "approx_timestamp": "31:50" },
222	    { "text": "Attempts at one, size constantly scaling up, streak constantly increasing... and you'll drop your presence down to one.", "approx_timestamp": "31:56" },
223	    { "text": "The best Outloop agentic coders have a presence of two. You show up at the prompt and you show up at the review.", "approx_timestamp": "32:15" },
224	    { "text": "First, go after chores, then go after bugs, then go after features... solve these stupid, simple problems that waste your time.", "approx_timestamp": "33:07" },
225	    { "text": "If you don't invest into the agentic layer of your codebase, how will you know when agents can solve your problem class end to end with no oversight?", "approx_timestamp": "37:25" },
226	    { "text": "I can guarantee you right now, you are doing engineering work you do not have to do. I can tell you that as a fact.", "approx_timestamp": "37:40" },
227	    { "text": "Everything starts small and then it compounds... they'll do it five times in a row, and you'll realize that you add no value by reviewing. In fact, you slowed things down.", "approx_timestamp": "37:53" },
228	    { "text": "They write a single prompt, hit enter and ship into production. Zero touch engineering. 90% of the time, there's no issues. And that number keeps going up — every tool release, every model release, every time they improve their agentic layer.", "approx_timestamp": "39:52" },
229	    { "text": "The real challenge I have for you in this course is about your belief. You have to believe that the agentic layer is worth investing into... If you don't believe that your agents can run your codebase, you're cooked.", "approx_timestamp": "41:10" },
230	    { "text": "It's not about being right. It's about being prepared to win. It's about thinking in the gray so that you can get the gains as soon as they're available.", "approx_timestamp": "41:35" },
231	    { "text": "The secret of tactical agentic coding is that it's not about the software developer lifecycle at all. It's about composable agentic primitives you can use to solve any engineering problem class.", "approx_timestamp": "45:58" },
232	    { "text": "The software developer lifecycle is powerful, but it's a remnant of the past... There's no doubt in my mind, it is not the optimal way to run software with agents.", "approx_timestamp": "46:26" },
233	    { "text": "This arrangement of ADWs is completely arbitrary. There is no one way to do this. The one way is the way that ships in your codebase.", "approx_timestamp": "47:20" },
234	    { "text": "It's deployed to production. The issue is closed. All I did was write this prompt: update the background color.", "approx_timestamp": "48:31" },
235	    { "text": "Don't run toward the future, don't walk toward it, sprint into the future.", "approx_timestamp": "49:06" },
236	    { "text": "The agentic layer is the highest leverage point in your codebase. This is the place where 1x input becomes 10x output, and 10x input becomes 100x if you invest in this layer.", "approx_timestamp": "49:44" },
237	    { "text": "The primitives are the atoms of agentic engineering. Master them and you can build any molecular structure you need.", "approx_timestamp": "51:37" }

249	    "The velocity scale has three levels — in-loop, out-loop, ZTE — measured by presence: continuous → two touchpoints (prompt + review) → one (prompt only).",
250	    "ZTE is PITER minus the R: same prompt input, trigger, environment — review is embedded into the pipeline (tests + agentic review + gates) instead of performed by you.",
251	    "The move to ZTE is evidence-gated per problem class: KPIs (attempts=1, rising streak) prove your review stopped adding value for that class. It is never a global switch.",
252	    "Parallel agents need isolation: worktree + branch + ports + state per run. The specific isolation tech (worktrees, Docker, VMs, E2B) is interchangeable; the capability is not.",
253	    "State objects (adw_state.json) are how single-purpose agents compose into pipelines without sharing a context window — and ship's completeness check turns that state into a go/no-go gate.",
254	    "Model sets are IDKs for compute allocation: one keyword in the issue re-maps which model each slash command runs — escalate implementation/debugging to opus, keep classification on sonnet.",
255	    "Review's question is 'is what we built what we asked for?' — proof of value (screenshots, and next: video) posted to your review system, not a human re-test.",
256	    "Dangerous automation deserves explicit interlocks: the ZTE workflow requires uppercase 'ZTE' to run; lowercase silently downgrades to reviewed SDLC.",
257	    "The SDLC arrangement is arbitrary packaging. The durable asset is the primitive set — templates, plans, prompts, ADW steps — composed per problem class ('the one way is the way that ships in your codebase').",
258	    "TAC-6 still holds at scale: one agent, one prompt, one purpose — more precision than stacking everything into one context window.",
259	    "The bottleneck migrates: stop coding (TAC-1) → your typing was the bottleneck; target ZTE (TAC-7) → your reviewing is next.",
260	    "The final hurdle is belief backed by measurement: invest, instrument, and let your own KPIs tell you when to drop the review."

{
  "lesson_key": "tac-7-zte-secret-of-agentic-engineering",
  "title": "ZTE Secret of Agentic Engineering",
  "course": "TAC",
  "order": 7,
  "lesson_url": "https://agenticengineer.com/tactical-agentic-coding/course/zte-secret-of-agentic-engineering",
  "lesson_subtitle": "Understand the North Star of Agentic Coding where your codebase ships itself. Progress from in loop, to out loop, to ZTE.",
  "level": "Advanced (lesson #7 of 8, second-to-last)",
  "video": {
    "file": "tac-7-zte-secret-of-agentic-engineering/video/tac-7-zte-secret-of-agentic-engineering.mp4",
    "duration_seconds": 3200,
    "duration_display": "53:20"
  },
  "tactic": {
    "name": "Target Zero-Touch Engineering",
    "one_liner": "Build your out-loop system so reliable that human review becomes a bottleneck, not a safety net — then drop the review: presence goes from two touchpoints (prompt + review) to one (prompt only), and work flows directly from prompt to production.",
    "why_uncomfortable": "TAC-1 asked you to stop coding; TAC-7 asks you to stop reviewing — the last place engineers feel indispensable. Dan names the reaction in-lesson: 'I know you're probably O-faced right now... Dan, absolutely no way, that's crazy. This isn't a real production application.' He agrees the demo app is a toy, then argues that objection misses the point: ZTE is a North Star you earn one problem class at a time (chores → bugs → features), and it only becomes available to engineers who invested in the agentic layer deeply enough to discover their review adds no value. It is 'YOLO mode for your AI developer workflows... maximum confidence mode' — deliberately provocative, deliberately gated (in the repo, the ZTE workflow literally refuses to run unless 'ZTE' is typed in uppercase).",
    "course_page_definition": "Zero-Touch Engineering is the third level of agentic coding beyond in-loop and out-loop, where your presence KPI drops from two touchpoints (prompt and review) to just one (prompt only). At this level, you witness something most engineers dismiss as impossible - a codebase that nearly runs itself. Your agents ship end-to-end with such reliability that human review becomes a bottleneck, not a safety net, allowing work to flow directly from prompt to production.",
    "daily_actions_from_course_card": [
      "Build parallel agent pipelines using isolated environments",
      "Scale from single agent to multi-agent workflows",
      "Create isolated environments for simultaneous execution",
      "Go from PITER to PITE with one prompt agentic workflows",
      "Build ADWs so great your review step becomes irrelevant"
    ]
  },
  "mission": "Collect the dividends of the complete end-to-end out-loop system built across TAC 1–6: hand five net-new pieces of work to the agentic layer and watch it plan, build, test, review, and document in parallel; scale beyond one agent with git-worktree isolation; add compute knobs (model sets); then confront the moment when you — the reviewer — become the bottleneck, and meet the third level of the Agentic Engineering Velocity Scale: Zero-Touch Engineering. Finally, receive the course's secret: none of this was ever about the SDLC — it's about composable agentic primitives that solve any engineering problem class.",
  "velocity_scale": {
    "name": "Agentic Engineering Velocity Scale (on-screen slide at 1:40)",
    "level1_in_loop": "In-loop agentic coding: you prompt interactively inside an agentic coding tool, watch, iterate, retest. Where most engineers operate. Presence is continuous. Dan: 'In-loop agentic coding is the lowest hanging fruit. Do not remain here.'",
    "level2_out_loop": "Out-loop: your engineering is templated into ADWs fired by triggers (GitHub issues → webhook). You appear exactly twice — at the prompt and at the review. 'The best out-loop agentic coders have a presence of two.' Out-loop systems beat out-of-the-box agentic tools because they contain YOUR engineering practices and workflows.",
    "level3_zte": "Zero-Touch Engineering: presence drops to one (the prompt). The pipeline plans, builds, tests, reviews, documents, and ships to production with no human review. PITER loses its R and becomes PITE. Earned per problem class, not switched on globally.",
    "not_binary": "Dan repeatedly guards against black-and-white reading: 'It's not in loop versus out loop. It's in loop moving toward out loop' (9:42), and mid-demo he deliberately goes back in-loop to review the drag-and-drop PR — 'think in the gray.'"
  },
  "piter_to_pite": {
    "recap": "PITER (from TAC-4, AFK agents): Prompt input → Trigger → Environment → Review. In TAC-7 the prompt input is GitHub issues, the trigger is a webhook (or 20-second cron poll), the environment is a dedicated always-on machine (Dan's Mac mini) plus per-run git worktrees, and the review is GitHub issue comments + uploaded screenshots + PRs.",
    "the_drop": "ZTE removes the R: 'You'll drop yourself off the end of the out-loop PITER framework and it becomes PITE, not PITER. You'll drop off the review' (31:19–31:26; the transcript mis-hears it as \"Pete not Peter\"). The course card states it as a daily action: 'Go from PITER to PITE with one prompt agentic workflows.'"
  },
  "secret": {
    "statement": "The secret of Tactical Agentic Coding: it's not about the software developer lifecycle at all. It's about composable agentic primitives you can use to solve any engineering problem class. (Stated twice verbatim, 45:58–46:10.)",
    "sdlc_demoted": "'The software developer lifecycle is powerful, but it's a remnant of the past... It is not the optimal way to run software with agents' (46:26). Plan/build/test/review/document was 'a package for me to deliver a message to you' — one arbitrary arrangement of primitives. 'There is no one way to do this. The one way is the way that ships in your codebase.'",
    "primitives_slide": "The 46:05 slide 'The Secret: Composable Agentic Primitives' draws three columns: Agentic Primitives (ADWs, Templates, Plans, Architecture, Tests, Documentation, Types, Standard Out, Tools, Prompt, Model, Context) → ADW steps (Plan, Build, Test, Review, Document, Deploy) → Composed Workflows (Plan→Build→Test, Build→Review→Deploy, Test→Document, ANY WORKFLOW).",
    "bridge_to_tac8": "Lesson 8 blows this open: 'The primitives are the atoms of agentic engineering. Master them and you can build any molecular structure you need' (51:37) — revisiting the atoms, then compositions across codebase types (web app, CLI tools, notebooks)."
  },
  "core_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "agentic-layer-payback",
      "name": "Collecting dividends from the agentic layer",
      "plain_english": "The lesson opens by cashing in on everything built in TAC 1–6: five net-new pieces of work (three features, a chore, a bug) are handed to the agentic layer as GitHub issues and shipped end-to-end while Dan reviews the codebase. The point is leverage realized: 'I parallelized myself across five features.'",
      "dan_words": "\"Let's collect the incredible dividends from our complete end to end Outloop agentic system... once you've built the system that builds the system, it's going to pay you back massively.\"",
      "misconception": "That this is a new build. Almost nothing in the demo is new machinery — it is TAC-4's PITER + TAC-5's closed loops + TAC-6's focused agents, now running all at once, in parallel, on real work."
    },
    {
      "id": "velocity-scale",
      "name": "The three levels: in-loop → out-loop → ZTE",
      "plain_english": "A named scale for how present you are in the work. In-loop: you drive interactively. Out-loop: systems drive; you show up at prompt and review (presence 2). ZTE: you show up at the prompt only (presence 1). The lesson's arc is earning the right to move right on this scale.",
      "dan_words": "\"There are three levels: in loop, out loop, and one additional level that we're going to break down in this lesson... first we're in the loop, next we're out the loop, and then we're doing ZTE — zero touch engineering.\"",
      "misconception": "Treating the scale as a switch instead of a gradient. Dan: 'This isn't black and white... It's in loop moving toward out loop. One day at a time.' He goes back in-loop on camera to review the drag-and-drop PR."
    },
    {
      "id": "worktree-isolation",
      "name": "Git worktrees: parallel agents on one device",
      "plain_english": "Every ADW run gets its own complete copy of the repo at trees/<adw_id>/ via git worktree (branched from origin/main), its own git branch, its own .ports.env, and its own backend/frontend ports (9100–9114 / 9200–9214, hashed from the ADW ID, 15 concurrent slots). That's what lets five pipelines run simultaneously without stepping on each other — and you can jump into any of them with `code trees/<id>`.",
      "dan_words": "\"We've adjusted all of our workflows to create their own isolated trees... In every tree, the application exists for a specific agent to build in. This is the easiest way to parallelize your workflows.\"",
      "misconception": "Fixating on worktrees as THE answer. Dan pre-empts: 'It doesn't matter that you use Git work trees... individual VMs, Docker containers — I don't care how you scale up your agent environments, it only matters that you can.' (The repo even ships an E2B cloud-sandbox proof-of-concept in adws/adw_tests/sandbox_poc.py.)"
    },
    {
      "id": "install-worktree",
      "name": "Environment setup is itself an agent task (/install_worktree)",
      "plain_english": "A worktree isn't usable until it's installed like an engineer would install it: copy .env files, append port config, copy .mcp.json and playwright config and rewrite their paths to absolute, uv sync, bun install, reset the database. ADW does this by running the /install_worktree slash command inside the new worktree, passing worktree path + both ports as arguments.",
      "dan_words": "\"The work tree sets up every piece that we need to operate the codebase in a dedicated directory... We're installing as if we, the engineer, were operating. This is critical. Some type of configuration format like this is going to be really important.\"",
      "misconception": "Hand-waving environment setup. If agents can't reproduce your dev environment from scratch, parallel isolation dies at step zero — this command IS the 'engineer onboarding doc' turned executable."
    },
    {
      "id": "state-object",
      "name": "The ADW state object (adw_state.json)",
      "plain_english": "Each run persists a small JSON at agents/<adw_id>/adw_state.json with exactly ten fields: adw_id, issue_number, branch_name, plan_file, issue_class, worktree_path, backend_port, frontend_port, model_set, all_adws. Every phase loads it, adds what it learned, saves it — that's how independent scripts chain into one pipeline, how you resume/replay a run, and how ship validates that every prior phase actually happened.",
      "dan_words": "\"To combat some of the state management issues that you're going to run into, we do have this state.json object... expect to have to add some type of state object inside your dedicated agent environments. This truly frees your agent to do one thing extraordinarily well with all the context it needs, and it lets you jump in and replay what that agent has done.\"",
      "misconception": "Stuffing state into the agent's context window instead. The state object is code-side memory; agents stay single-purpose (TAC-6) precisely because the pipeline, not the prompt, carries the bookkeeping."
    },
    {
      "id": "one-agent-one-prompt-one-purpose",
      "name": "TAC-6's tactic survives the scale-up",
      "plain_english": "Parallelism did not merge agents into one mega-context. Each phase is still one agent running one prompt with a single purpose (sdlc_planner, sdlc_implementor, tester, reviewer, documenter, shipper) — now multiplied across worktrees.",
      "dan_words": "\"It's also important to mention that the lesson six tactic has not been broken. This is really important for scaling. We have one agent running one prompt with a single purpose... You have more precision while other engineers are trying to stack up into one context window.\"",
      "misconception": "Believing scale requires bigger agents. TAC scales by adding more isolated small agents, not by growing one agent's context."
    },
    {
      "id": "model-sets",
      "name": "Model sets: a compute knob encoded as an IDK",
      "plain_english": "Typing 'model_set heavy' in a GitHub issue changes which model every slash command runs on. agent.py holds SLASH_COMMAND_MODEL_MAP: all 18 commands run sonnet on base; on heavy, exactly 8 escalate to opus (/implement, /resolve_failed_test, /resolve_failed_e2e_test, /document, /chore, /bug, /feature, /patch) while classification/test/review/plumbing commands stay sonnet. Same prompts, same pipeline — more compute where it pays.",
      "dan_words": "\"We're adding a knob to our capabilities... Our model set changes the set of models that runs against our workflow... It gives us a little knob to turn to increase the compute that our workflow uses. You can encode any information dense keyword you want — you just have to make sure that your prompts recognize it and pick it up.\"",
      "misconception": "Thinking heavy = better everywhere. The map is deliberately selective: creative/implementation work escalates; deterministic parsing and classification don't. Compute allocation is itself an engineering decision you encode once."
    },
    {
      "id": "idk-plumbing",
      "name": "Where the knob gets read: /classify_adw at the top of every trigger",
      "plain_english": "The webhook hands the raw issue/comment text to the /classify_adw agent, which returns strict JSON: {adw_slash_command, adw_id, model_set}. That's how plain English in an issue selects a workflow, resumes an existing run by ID, and sets the model set — and where the safety interlock lives: the classifier is instructed to run the ZTE workflow only if 'ZTE' is explicitly uppercase, otherwise it downgrades to plain SDLC.",
      "dan_words": "\"If you're ever wondering where this stuff runs, you can always just type slash classify ADW... it runs right here, workflow operations, where we classify the ADW at the beginning of the workflow... We've encoded this and you can see we just use base or heavy.\"",
      "misconception": "Assuming triggers need rigid syntax. The classifier normalizes variations ('adw plan build', missing _iso suffix) — natural language in, validated enum out, with code-side validation against AVAILABLE_ADW_WORKFLOWS after."
    },
    {
      "id": "review-proof-of-value",
      "name": "Review = proof of value (screenshots posted to the issue)",
      "plain_english": "The review agent starts the app in the worktree on its allocated ports, drives it with Playwright MCP, takes 1–5 numbered screenshots of the critical paths, classifies any issues (skippable / tech_debt / blocker), and returns strict JSON. Screenshots are uploaded to a Cloudflare R2 public bucket and posted back onto the triggering GitHub issue — the agent proves the feature shipped without you leaving the review system.",
      "dan_words": "\"Our agents took images and gave us proof that the feature has shipped... Remember what the review step answers: it's not 'does it work?' It's 'is what we built what we asked for?' (21:40)... Having a comprehensive review system is a massive, massive edge for increasing your review velocity.\"",

  "sdlc_zte_pipeline": {

      "test_fail": "aborts with 'ZTE Aborted - Test phase failed' comment",
      "review_fail": "aborts with 'ZTE Aborted - Review phase failed' comment",

      "ship_fail": "posts 'ZTE Failed - Ship phase failed... merge manually if needed'"

    "zte_uppercase_interlock": ".claude/commands/classify_adw.md: 'DO NOT RUN the adw_sdlc_ZTE_iso workflows unless ZTE is EXPLICITLY uppercased.   "quotes": [
    { "text": "You'll witness something most engineers dismiss as impossible: a codebase that nearly runs itself.", "approx_timestamp": "0:28" },
    { "text": "We'll understand a critical moment in the future where human in the loop review becomes a bottleneck, not a safety net.", "approx_timestamp": "2:06" },
    { "text": "We're operating out the loop so we can scale our impact as easily as copying a file.", "approx_timestamp": "3:17" },
    { "text": "This is absurd levels of scale.", "approx_timestamp": "7:08" },
    { "text": "The ADW directory is a scripting layer that lets us construct pipelines of agents that solve specific classes of problems back to back to back.", "approx_timestamp": "9:18" },
    { "text": "This isn't black and white. It's not in loop versus out loop. It's in loop moving toward out loop.", "approx_timestamp": "9:40" },
    { "text": "I don't care how you scale up your agent environments, it only matters that you can.", "approx_timestamp": "11:40" },
    { "text": "We're not solving the problem directly anymore... the rate in which you can solve your specific problem can now be drastically scaled up when you put your effort into your agentic layer.", "approx_timestamp": "13:49" },
    { "text": "This truly frees your agent to do one thing extraordinarily well with all the context it needs, and it lets you jump in and replay what that agent has done.", "approx_timestamp": "15:01" },
    { "text": "You can encode any information dense keyword that you want. You just have to make sure that your prompts recognize it and pick it up.", "approx_timestamp": "16:04" },
    { "text": "Remember what the review step answers. It's not 'does it work?' It's 'is what we built what we asked for?'", "approx_timestamp": "21:40" },
    { "text": "Teach your agent how to do it once and then run it over and over and over again and scale it across your team.", "approx_timestamp": "24:48" },
    { "text": "You can't vibe code this stuff. Your agent is operating as you would. You've templated your engineering.", "approx_timestamp": "27:59" },
    { "text": "When the agents arrived, something changed. We weren't just AI coding anymore. We started orchestrating intelligence.", "approx_timestamp": "29:21" },
    { "text": "This human in the loop model is a bottleneck. I'm not catching any bugs anymore. I'm not adding any value outside of the agentic layer. I'm going to remove the human in the loop review process for this class of problems.", "approx_timestamp": "30:45" },
    { "text": "You'll drop yourself off the end of the Outloop PITER framework and it becomes PITE, not PITER. You'll drop off the review.", "approx_timestamp": "31:19" },
    { "text": "This is YOLO mode for your AI developer workflows... It's maximum confidence mode for agentic engineering. No review. Just like you've stopped coding, you'll stop reviewing.", "approx_timestamp": "31:33" },
    { "text": "This is the lesson seven tactic: Target zero touch engineering. This is the ultimate agentic coding North Star.", "approx_timestamp": "31:50" },
    { "text": "Attempts at one, size constantly scaling up, streak constantly increasing... and you'll drop your presence down to one.", "approx_timestamp": "31:56" },
    { "text": "The best Outloop agentic coders have a presence of two. You show up at the prompt and you show up at the review.", "approx_timestamp": "32:15" },
    { "text": "First, go after chores, then go after bugs, then go after features... solve these stupid, simple problems that waste your time.", "approx_timestamp": "33:07" },
    { "text": "If you don't invest into the agentic layer of your codebase, how will you know when agents can solve your problem class end to end with no oversight?", "approx_timestamp": "37:25" },
    { "text": "I can guarantee you right now, you are doing engineering work you do not have to do. I can tell you that as a fact.", "approx_timestamp": "37:40" },
    { "text": "Everything starts small and then it compounds... they'll do it five times in a row, and you'll realize that you add no value by reviewing. In fact, you slowed things down.", "approx_timestamp": "37:53" },
    { "text": "They write a single prompt, hit enter and ship into production. Zero touch engineering. 90% of the time, there's no issues. And that number keeps going up — every tool release, every model release, every time they improve their agentic layer.", "approx_timestamp": "39:52" },
    { "text": "The real challenge I have for you in this course is about your belief. You have to believe that the agentic layer is worth investing into... If you don't believe that your agents can run your codebase, you're cooked.", "approx_timestamp": "41:10" },
    { "text": "It's not about being right. It's about being prepared to win. It's about thinking in the gray so that you can get the gains as soon as they're available.", "approx_timestamp": "41:35" },
    { "text": "The secret of tactical agentic coding is that it's not about the software developer lifecycle at all. It's about composable agentic primitives you can use to solve any engineering problem class.", "approx_timestamp": "45:58" },
    { "text": "The software developer lifecycle is powerful, but it's a remnant of the past... There's no doubt in my mind, it is not the optimal way to run software with agents.", "approx_timestamp": "46:26" },
    { "text": "This arrangement of ADWs is completely arbitrary. There is no one way to do this. The one way is the way that ships in your codebase.", "approx_timestamp": "47:20" },
    { "text": "It's deployed to production. The issue is closed. All I did was write this prompt: update the background color.", "approx_timestamp": "48:31" },
    { "text": "Don't run toward the future, don't walk toward it, sprint into the future.", "approx_timestamp": "49:06" },
    { "text": "The agentic layer is the highest leverage point in your codebase. This is the place where 1x input becomes 10x output, and 10x input becomes 100x if you invest in this layer.", "approx_timestamp": "49:44" },
    { "text": "The primitives are the atoms of agentic engineering. Master them and you can build any molecular structure you need.", "approx_timestamp": "51:37" }

  "what_student_must_internalize": [
    "The velocity scale has three levels — in-loop, out-loop, ZTE — measured by presence: continuous → two touchpoints (prompt + review) → one (prompt only).",
    "ZTE is PITER minus the R: same prompt input, trigger, environment — review is embedded into the pipeline (tests + agentic review + gates) instead of performed by you.",
    "The move to ZTE is evidence-gated per problem class: KPIs (attempts=1, rising streak) prove your review stopped adding value for that class. It is never a global switch.",
    "Parallel agents need isolation: worktree + branch + ports + state per run. The specific isolation tech (worktrees, Docker, VMs, E2B) is interchangeable; the capability is not.",
    "State objects (adw_state.json) are how single-purpose agents compose into pipelines without sharing a context window — and ship's completeness check turns that state into a go/no-go gate.",
    "Model sets are IDKs for compute allocation: one keyword in the issue re-maps which model each slash command runs — escalate implementation/debugging to opus, keep classification on sonnet.",
    "Review's question is 'is what we built what we asked for?' — proof of value (screenshots, and next: video) posted to your review system, not a human re-test.",
    "Dangerous automation deserves explicit interlocks: the ZTE workflow requires uppercase 'ZTE' to run; lowercase silently downgrades to reviewed SDLC.",
    "The SDLC arrangement is arbitrary packaging. The durable asset is the primitive set — templates, plans, prompts, ADW steps — composed per problem class ('the one way is the way that ships in your codebase').",
    "TAC-6 still holds at scale: one agent, one prompt, one purpose — more precision than stacking everything into one context window.",
    "The bottleneck migrates: stop coding (TAC-1) → your typing was the bottleneck; target ZTE (TAC-7) → your reviewing is next.",
    "The final hurdle is belief backed by measurement: invest, instrument, and let your own KPIs tell you when to drop the review."
  ],

    { "q": "What is Tactic #7?", "a": "Target Zero-Touch Engineering — build ADWs so reliable that human review becomes a bottleneck, then remove it and let agents ship prompt-to-production. It's a North Star you target per problem class, not a switch." },
    { "q": "What does PITER become under ZTE and why?", "a": "PITE — the R (review) is dropped because review is embedded in the pipeline (tests, agentic review with screenshots, state validation) instead of performed by a human." },
    { "q": "What four things isolate one ADW run from another in tac-7?", "a": "Its own git worktree (trees/<adw_id>, a full repo copy), its own branch ({class}-issue-{n}-adw-{id}-{slug}), its own ports (backend 9100–9114, frontend 9200–9214, derived from the ADW ID; 15 concurrent slots), and its own state file (agents/<adw_id>/adw_state.json)." },
    { "q": "List the ten fields of adw_state.json.", "a": "adw_id, issue_number, branch_name, plan_file, issue_class, worktree_path, backend_port, frontend_port, model_set, all_adws." },
    { "q": "What phases does adw_sdlc_zte_iso run, and which failure does NOT block shipping?", "a": "Plan → build → test → review → document → ship. Test or review failure aborts ZTE; documentation failure only warns — the run continues to ship." },
    { "q": "How does the ship phase actually merge to main?", "a": "It validates all eight required state fields and the worktree, then in the main repo root: git fetch, checkout main, pull, git merge --no-ff <feature-branch>, git push origin main. (The adws/README's 'approve PR + squash' description is stale — the code does a manual no-ff merge.)" },
    { "q": "What safety interlock guards the ZTE workflow at the trigger level?", "a": "The /classify_adw prompt refuses to select adw_sdlc_ZTE_iso unless 'ZTE' is explicitly uppercase in the issue text; lowercase 'zte' downgrades to the reviewed adw_sdlc_iso." },
    { "q": "What is a model set, and which commands escalate on 'heavy'?", "a": "An information-dense keyword (model_set base|heavy) stored in state that re-maps each slash command's model via SLASH_COMMAND_MODEL_MAP. On heavy, 8 of 18 commands switch sonnet→opus: /implement, /resolve_failed_test, /resolve_failed_e2e_test, /document, /chore, /bug, /feature, /patch. Classification, testing, review, commit, PR plumbing stay on sonnet." },
    { "q": "What question does the review step answer, and how does it prove its answer?", "a": "'Is what we built what we asked for?' (not 'does it work' — tests answered that). It drives the app in the worktree via Playwright MCP, takes 1–5 numbered screenshots of critical paths, classifies issues as skippable/tech_debt/blocker, uploads screenshots to Cloudflare R2, and posts them on the GitHub issue." },
    { "q": "How do the agentic KPIs tell you a problem class is ZTE-ready?", "a": "Attempts pinned at 1, streak (consecutive runs with attempts ≤ 2) climbing, size scaling up — while your reviews stop catching anything. Dan's threshold sketch: ~90% confidence a class ships with no issues, 'and that number keeps going up.'" },
    { "q": "Which two triggers can start ADWs, and what prevents infinite webhook loops?", "a": "A FastAPI webhook (POST /gh-webhook, port 8001, instant) and a cron poller (every 20 seconds). Every bot comment embeds the [ADW-AGENTS] identifier, and the webhook ignores any payload containing it." },
    { "q": "Do browser E2E tests run inside adw_sdlc_iso / adw_sdlc_zte_iso?", "a": "No — both orchestrators hardcode --skip-e2e ('Always skip E2E tests in SDLC workflows'). Unit tests gate the pipeline; E2E runs only via a standalone adw_test_iso without the flag." },
    { "q": "What is the secret of Tactical Agentic Coding?", "a": "It's not about the software developer lifecycle at all — it's about composable agentic primitives you can use to solve any engineering problem class. The SDLC arrangement is 'completely arbitrary... a package to deliver a message'; the one way is the way that ships in your codebase." },
    { "q": "What does Dan say is the real hurdle of TAC, and his four postures toward the future?", "a": "Belief — 'you have to believe the agentic layer is worth investing into... if you don't believe your agents can run your codebase, you're cooked.' Postures: run away, stand still, move toward it, or sprint ('sprint into the future')." },

"adws/adw_modules/workflow_ops.py": "Shared ops: extract_adw_info via /classify_adw, classify_issue (/chore|/bug|/feature), build_plan, implement_plan, create_commit, create_pull_request, ensure_adw_id, find/create branch, AVAILABLE_ADW_WORKFLOWS runtime validation, [ADW-AGENTS]-prefixed issue messaging.",
      "adws/adw_triggers/trigger_webhook.py": "FastAPI receiver (port 8001): filters bot comments, requires 'adw_' text, classifies, blocks dependent workflows without adw_id, persists state, posts the detection comment, launches the workflow detached (Popen, start_new_session) to answer GitHub within 10s. /health runs the full system health check.",
      "adws/adw_triggers/trigger_cron.py": "Polling alternative: every 20 seconds; fires on new comment-less issues or a latest comment of exactly 'adw'.",
      "adws/adw_modules/r2_uploader.py": "Cloudflare R2 uploads for review screenshots (boto3 S3 API); returns public URLs (default domain tac-public-imgs.iddagents.com) that get embedded in issue comments; silently disables without credentials.",
      ".claude/commands/classify_adw.md": "Extracts {adw_slash_command, adw_id, model_set} as strict JSON from free text; normalizes command variants; carries the uppercase-ZTE interlock.",
      ".claude/commands/install_worktree.md": "Agent-run environment installer: .ports.env, .env copies + port appends, .mcp.json/playwright config copies with absolute-path rewrites, uv sync, bun install, DB reset, and a full report contract.",
      ".claude/commands/in_loop_review.md": "The deliberate step back into the loop: fetch + checkout branch, prepare_app (DB reset + start), open localhost for hands-on inspection.",
      ".claude/commands/track_agentic_kpis.md": "Maintains app_docs/agentic_kpis.md: per-run rows (attempts from all_adws, plan size via wc -l, diff via git diff --shortstat) and summary metrics (current/longest streak with attempts ≤ 2, totals, average presence) — all arithmetic forced through python -c.",
      ".claude/commands/review.md": "Spec-vs-implementation review: 1–5 numbered screenshots via Playwright MCP, severity taxonomy (skippable/tech_debt/blocker), success = no blockers, strict-JSON output contract ('we'll immediately run JSON.parse()').",
      ".claude/commands/conditional_docs.md": "Condition → documentation routing table; the document phase appends new feature docs here so future agents self-serve the right context ('this lets our agents scale with the size of our codebase').",
      ".claude/settings.json": "Interactive-session permissions (deny git push --force / rm -rf) + all seven hook wirings (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Notification, Stop, SubagentStop, PreCompact, UserPromptSubmit).",
      "app_docs/agentic_kpis.md": "Committed KPI evidence: run cc73faf1 (issue #47, /chore, attempts 1, plan 39 lines, diff 274/5/10, average presence 1.0, streak 1) — a real ZTE run's paper trail.",
      "specs/issue-47-adw-cc73faf1-sdlc_planner-update-upload-button.md": "Committed plan whose metadata preserves the actual ZTE trigger: issue body '/chore adw_sdlc_ZTE_iso - update Upload Data to be Upload'.",
      "app/server/core/llm_processor.py": "The demo app's NL→SQL brain (gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 / claude-sonnet-4-0 in the shipped snapshot — the target of the on-video 'bump to o4-mini' chore, whose review reported 78 tests passing).",
      "ai_docs/ (5 files)": "Pinned third-party context for agents: anthropic_quick_start, claude_code_cli_reference, claude_code_sdk, openai_quick_start, e2b (the containerization alternative Dan name-checks)."
    },
    "generated_not_committed": {
      "trees/<adw_id>/": "Per-run worktrees (full repo copies); gitignored; created by plan/patch entry points, removed by scripts/purge_tree.sh.",
      "agents/<adw_id>/** (fresh runs)": "State, per-agent prompts, raw_output.jsonl/json session logs, reviewer review_img/ screenshots — five historical run dirs are committed as evidence.",

      "logs/<session_id>/": "Hook logs per Claude Code session (LOG_BASE_DIR)."
    }

4	
5	---
6	
7	## Tier 1 — If you remember nothing else
8	
9	**1. The whole upgrade is ONE added ingredient.**
10	AI coding runs on the big three: **context, model, prompt**. Agentic coding = big three + **tools**, and "tools" means *prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tool calls*. That's the core four. Every lesson after this one is just scaling that fourth ingredient.
11	*Why weak learners lose it:* it sounds too small to matter. Test yourself: when a run fails, can you name which of the four was wrong?
12	
13	**2. Stop coding ≠ stop shipping code, and ≠ stop reading code.**
14	Stop *typing* it. Agents type; you plan, review, and build closed loops. Code volume goes UP; your keystrokes go to zero. If you hand-edit the agent's file when it's 90% right instead of re-prompting, you've quietly quit the course.
15	*Say it Dan's way:* "Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code. Full stop."
16	
17	**3. A prompt can BE a workflow.**
18	The README's agentic prompt isn't a request for text — it's a runbook: RUN (branch) → CREATE (file) → RUN (execute, add, commit). The agent plans it as a checklist and does engineering work. If you can only remember one artifact from the lesson, remember what those 12 lines did.
19	
20	**4. The agent is a function you can call from code.**
21	`claude -p "<prompt>"` from shell, Python, or TypeScript. Three tiny scripts in `programmable/` prove it. This is the seed of everything "systems that build systems" means — the agent stops being a chat window and becomes a building block you can embed anywhere, including places you aren't.
22	
23	---
24	
25	## Tier 2 — The working machinery
26	
27	**5. The A/B test is the lesson. Run it, don't watch it.**
28	Same repo, two prompts: `main_aic.py` (file generated — phase 1) vs branch+file+runs+commit+report (engineering done — phase 2). Then delete the branch and rerun it *headlessly* with `uv run python programmable/programmable.py`. Feeling the rerun is what installs the concept.
29	
30	**6. Read `.claude/settings.json` before you run anything. Always.**
31	It's the agent's entire tool surface: Read/Write/Edit, `uv run`, four git commands, WebSearch. Know what the agent MAY do and you can predict everything it will do. This habit scales to every agentic tool you'll ever touch.
32	
33	**7. "Tool calling isn't new" — correct, and irrelevant.**
34	Dan's rebuttal, verbatim: "It's not a question of new. It's a question of **scale and performance**." What's new is *reliable long chains*: plans that survive twelve consecutive tool calls without derailing.
35	
36	**8. Why Claude Code (three essential elements).**
37	(1) A model that can reason when needed, (2) consistent long tool chains, (3) the right agent architecture. Together they made "reliable agentic coding at scale" possible for the first time. Use the trio as a checklist for judging ANY agentic tool — that's the transferable part. Don't get stuck on any one tool.
38	
39	**9. Make the agent REPORT.**
40	`programmable/prompt.md` ends with `REPORT: respond with the exact output of both .py files`. Headless work you can't verify is work you can't trust. Report-back is the first closed-loop habit of the course.
41	
42	**10. Wrapped in the right tool, prompts become long-running workflows.**
43	Minutes to hours, end to end, with and without your oversight — fired repeatedly with the right triggers at the right time. That's the scale Dan is asking you not to turn your brain off about.
44	
45	---
46	
47	## Tier 3 — Framing that keeps you going
48	
49	**11. You're an engineer, not a coder.**
50	Engineering was never about writing code; it's about systems of leverage that produce outcomes for users and customers. This reframe is what makes Tactic #1 survivable emotionally.
51	
52	**12. 10x comes from leverage, never from effort.**
53	And the number is arbitrary — 2x, 10x, 100x — set by the leverage points you find. 80% of life is noise and repetition; this is the rare opportunity worth focusing on.
54	
55	**13. Pay to play.**
56	Millions and millions of tokens across the course. Budget for it (plan or API funds) or you'll stall mid-lesson and blame the tactics.
57	
58	**14. The contradicting truth: to become irreplaceable, replace yourself.**
59	Whoever automates the work owns the automation. What gets replaced is your typing; what becomes irreplaceable is your judgment and your ownership of the systems doing the work.
60	
61	**15. The mission has named enemies.**
62	"An engineer *they* can't replace — your boss, the company, the industry, AI." Nothing in tech is forever; constant evolution is the price of staying valuable. That's why lesson 1 spends six minutes on stakes before touching a terminal.
63	
64	---
65	
66	## Micro-quiz (close the book first)
67	
68	1. Big three? Core four? Which element is new and what's its precise definition?
69	2. Five things the agentic prompt did that the AI coding prompt didn't?
70	3. What file tells you the agent's tool surface, and what's in it here?
71	4. Write the shell version of the programmable pattern from memory (3 lines).
72	5. What does prompt.md's REPORT block demand, and why does that matter for headless runs?
73	6. Resolve the paradox: how does replacing yourself make you irreplaceable?
74

---

## Tier 2 — The working machinery

**5. The A/B test is the lesson. Run it, don't watch it.**

**8. Why Claude Code (three essential elements).**

Use the trio as a checklist for judging ANY agentic tool — that's the transferable part. Don't get stuck on any one tool.

---

## Tier 3 — Framing that keeps you going

**11. You're an engineer, not a coder.**
Engineering was never about writing code; it's about systems of leverage that produce outcomes for users and customers. This reframe is what makes Tactic #1 survivable emotionally.

**12. 10x comes from leverage, never from effort.**
And the number is arbitrary — 2x, 10x, 100x — set by the leverage points you find. 80% of life is noise and repetition; this is the rare opportunity worth focusing on.

**13. Pay to play.**
Millions and millions of tokens across the course. Budget for it (plan or API funds) or you'll stall mid-lesson and blame the tactics.

**14. The contradicting truth: to become irreplaceable, replace yourself.**
Whoever automates the work owns the automation. What gets replaced is your typing; what becomes irreplaceable is your judgment and your ownership of the systems doing the work.

**15. The mission has named enemies.**
"An engineer *they* can't replace — your boss, the company, the industry, AI." Nothing in tech is forever; constant evolution is the price of staying valuable. That's why lesson 1 spends six minutes on stakes before touching a terminal.

1	# TAC-1 — Outdated vs Current (course era → mid-2026)
2	
3	TAC-1 ages unusually well because it teaches primitives, and Dan future-proofs on camera: *"Your Claude Code UI might look different. You might be using newer models. That's all great... Don't let that distract you from the value embedded in each lesson."* Still, five things have moved. For each: what the course shows, what current practice is, and whether the book needs an overlay.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## 1. Reusable agent behavior: prompt files → Agent Skills  ⟵ the big named gap
8	
9	**Course era:** reusable behavior is encoded as a raw prompt file (`programmable/prompt.md`) plus launcher scripts. Works, but discovery, triggering, and composition are all manual.
10	**Current:** Agent Skills are the first-class encoding — `SKILL.md` files with frontmatter (name, description, trigger guidance), loaded on demand by Claude Code and shareable across projects/teams. Skills are the modern answer to "how do I package the thing my agent knows how to do?" — exactly the question `programmable/` answers primitively.
11	**Book treatment:** overlay REQUIRED. This is the course's most-cited gap ("Skills as modern encoding of engineering"). Teach prompt.md first (pedagogically perfect: no magic), then show the same workflow as a Skill.
12	**Overlay:** `X2ciJedw2vU` — *RAW Agentic Coding: ZERO to Agent SKILL* (include_in_phase1: **yes**).
13	
14	## 2. Embedding: bare `claude -p` → headless mode + Claude Agent SDK
15	
16	**Course era:** `claude -p "<prompt>"` via subprocess from sh/ts/py; output captured as plain text; REPORT requested inside the prompt itself.
17	**Current:** the pattern survives verbatim (and remains the best teaching form), but production embedding now uses headless flags — `--output-format json|stream-json`, `--allowedTools`, `--permission-mode`, session resume — and, for real systems, the Claude Agent SDK (Python/TS): structured outputs, hooks, subagents, multi-turn control. What TAC-1 calls "programmable agentic coding" grew into a supported product surface.
18	**Book treatment:** sidebar ("the 3-line script you just wrote has a grown-up form"), not a rewrite — concept unchanged: agent as callable component.
19	**Overlay:** `6fCqj4xFCZI` — *How Claude Code CHANGED Engineering Forever* (include_in_phase1: **yes**).
20	
21	## 3. Permissions: flat allowlist → modes, hooks, sandboxing
22	
23	**Course era:** `.claude/settings.json` with a flat `permissions.allow` list (`Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `Bash(uv run:*)`, four git patterns, `WebSearch`).
24	**Current:** that syntax still works, but the surface grew: permission modes (plan/accept-edits/etc.), pre/post tool-use hooks, sandboxed bash, deny rules, and settings layering (user/project/local). Teams gate agents with hooks, not just allowlists.
25	**Book treatment:** footnote + "current practice" callout. The lesson's HABIT — always read what the agent may do before running it — transfers unchanged and is the actual teaching point.
26	**Overlay:** none needed.
27	
28	## 4. Models & UI: period detail, pre-handled by Dan
29	
30	**Course era:** course-era Claude models and TUI; Aider cited as the phase-1 analogue.
31	**Current:** newer model families (Claude 4.x → Claude 5 era), richer TUI, plan modes, background tasks. None of it invalidates a frame of the lesson — the demo is deliberately primitive-level.
32	**Book treatment:** one-line margin note on affected screenshots ("UI is period detail; the flow is identical today"). No overlay.
33	
34	## 5. Scale: one serial loop → fleets, subagents, parallel worktrees
35	
36	**Course era:** one agent, one workflow, serially, in one terminal — deliberately, since it's lesson 1 of 8.
37	**Current:** the same agentic prompt is routinely fanned out: subagents, background tasks, git-worktree-isolated parallel runs, orchestrated pipelines. "Systems that build systems" now has industrial-strength machinery.
38	**Book treatment:** forward-pointer only ("the course scales this in later lessons; today's ceiling is higher still"). Overlaying scale content on lesson 1 would front-run the pedagogy.
39	**Overlay candidates (deferred to later chapters):** `fop_yxV-mPo` — *Codebase Singularity*; `hGg3nWp7afg` — *3 Codebase Folders* (both include_in_phase1: **no**).
40	
41	---
42	
43	## What has NOT aged (teach with full confidence)
44	
45	- The phase-1/phase-2 frame and "AI coding is not enough" — if anything, more consensus now than at recording.
46	- The core four. Context/model/prompt/tools remains the complete diagnostic vocabulary for agentic failures.
47	- The agentic prompt as workflow-specification (RUN/CREATE/RUN/REPORT) — this shape is now everywhere (slash commands, skills, CI prompts).
48	- "Scale and performance, not novelty" as the right lens on tool calling.
49	- The three-essential-elements checklist for evaluating agentic tools.
50	- Terminal ubiquity as the embedding superpower.
51	- Report-back as the first closed-loop habit.
52	- The economics: token spend as pay-to-play. (Costs shifted; the logic didn't.)
53	
54	## Phase-1 overlay decision (strict, per brief: max 1–3)
55	
56	| # | Video | Maps to | Include |
57	|---|---|---|---|
58	| 1 | `2TIXl2rlA6Q` — AI Coding is NOT ENOUGH | operationalizes tactic (lesson thesis, phase model) | ✅ |
59	| 2 | `6fCqj4xFCZI` — How Claude Code CHANGED Engineering Forever | named hole (form factor + programmable embedding, current state) | ✅ |
60	| 3 | `X2ciJedw2vU` — RAW Agentic Coding: ZERO to Agent SKILL | corrects outdated (skills gap) | ✅ |
61	| 4 | `fop_yxV-mPo` — Codebase Singularity | self-operating vision → later lessons | ❌ defer |
62	| 5 | `hGg3nWp7afg` — 3 Codebase Folders | context engineering → later lessons | ❌ defer |
63	
64	*Caveat: IDs/titles from the orchestration brief's seed list; verify each resolves and content matches title before publishing overlay links (no video fetching was performed in this extract pass, per brief).*

# TAC-1 Lab Spec — Hello Agentic Coding

**Scope rule:** every drill runs inside the course codebase only (`codebase/` → `tac/tac-1`; students: `git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-1.git`). No external repos, no extra dependencies beyond the lesson's prerequisite tools.
**Prime directive (graded throughout):** you type **zero** lines of application code by hand. Even file edits in the stretch drills go through Claude Code.
**Time box:** 45–75 minutes. Token cost: one interactive demo pair + 3–5 headless runs (small; but real — pay to play).

---

## 0 · Setup (10 min)

1. Fresh directory for TAC codebases → `git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-1.git && cd tac-1`
2. Verify the toolbelt: `claude --version`, `uv --version`, `git --version`; optional `bun --version` (TS variant). Windows: run everything inside WSL.
3. **Permissions audit (do not skip):** open `.claude/settings.json` and answer in writing:
   - Which three file tools may the agent use freely?
   - Which four git subcommands are allowed? Which git subcommands are NOT (e.g. `push`)?
   - What single non-local tool is enabled? (`WebSearch`)
4. Open the repo in your IDE, open the terminal (Cmd+J in VS Code), run `claude`.

**Checkpoint 0:** you can state, without looking, what the agent may do. If you can't, re-read the file — this habit is a graded outcome.

## 1 · Reproduce Dan — interactive A/B (15 min)

**A. Phase-1 prompt.** Copy the README **AI Coding Prompt** into Claude Code; fire.
- Verify: `main_aic.py` exists; `uv run main_aic.py` → `goodbye ai coding`.
- Note what did NOT happen: no branch, no commit, no execution by the agent.

**B. Phase-2 prompt.** Copy the README **Agentic Coding Prompt**; fire. Watch the todo checklist form, then drain.
- Verify all five engineering actions:
  1. `git branch --show-current` → `demo-agentic-coding`
  2. `main_tac.py` exists; `uv run main_tac.py` → `hello agentic coding` + one-line AI-agent definition
  3. both files were executed by the agent (outputs visible in its trace)
  4. `git log --oneline -1` → `Demo agentic coding capabilities`
  5. the agent reported what it did and cleaned up its todos

**Checkpoint 1 (write it down):** list the five actions prompt B performed that prompt A didn't. This list IS the AI-coding → agentic-coding delta.

## 2 · Reproduce Dan — programmable/headless (15 min)

1. Read `programmable/prompt.md`. Spot the two differences from the README agentic prompt *before* running anything: (a) it also CREATEs `main_aic.py` — self-contained, no dependency on drill 1; (b) it ends with a `REPORT:` block demanding the exact output of both .py files.
2. Clean slate exactly like Dan: `git checkout main && git branch -D demo-agentic-coding`
3. From a fresh terminal on `main`: `uv run python programmable/programmable.py` — hands off. No interaction allowed.
4. When it returns, verify: branch re-created, both files re-created, commit present, and the printed REPORT contains the exact outputs (cross-check by running both files yourself).
5. Run the same workflow via the other two launchers (reset the branch between runs):
   - `sh programmable/programmable.sh`
   - `bun run programmable/programmable.ts`

**Checkpoint 2:** all three launchers drove the identical workflow. Say in one sentence why the language didn't matter. *(Claude Code runs in the terminal; anything with terminal access can call `claude -p` — the agent is a function.)*

## 3 · Stretch drills (15–30 min, still zero hand-typing)

**S1 — Extend the REPORT (closed-loop thinking).** Using Claude Code (not your editor), edit `programmable/prompt.md` so REPORT also includes the current git branch name. Reset the branch; rerun the Python launcher; verify the report changed accordingly.

**S2 — Fourth launcher (prove the pattern).** Ask Claude Code to add a launcher in another language available on your machine (e.g. plain Node, Ruby, Go — anything with terminal access), following the existing three as style guides. Reset; run it; verify the identical workflow.

**S3 — Break the tool surface (permissions intuition).** Via Claude Code, remove `"Bash(git commit:*)"` from `.claude/settings.json`. Rerun the agentic prompt and observe precisely where and how the workflow halts or asks. Restore the permission. Write one sentence: what does this teach about the tools circle of the core four? *(The tool surface bounds what an agentic prompt can accomplish; permissions are part of the system design.)*

**S4 — Map to your job (transfer).** Time drill 1A and 1B. Then write two lists from your actual work: tasks that are AI-coding-prompt-shaped vs agentic-coding-prompt-shaped. Circle the one agentic-shaped task you'd automate first with the `programmable/` pattern.

## Pass criteria (all required)

- [ ] Zero application code typed by hand anywhere in the lab
- [ ] Permissions audit answers correct (checkpoint 0)
- [ ] Five-action delta list correct (checkpoint 1)
- [ ] `demo-agentic-coding` branch exists with commit `Demo agentic coding capabilities` containing `main_aic.py` + `main_tac.py`
- [ ] `uv run main_tac.py` prints "hello agentic coding" + a one-line AI-agent definition
- [ ] All three (or four, with S2) launchers completed headlessly with a REPORT matching the real outputs
- [ ] Closing oral check, no notes: the core four; the one-dimension delta; Claude Code's three essential elements; the contradicting truth resolved in one sentence

## Instructor / self-check notes

- **Most common stall:** the "new/existing branch" wording — if the branch already exists from a prior run, the agent may reuse it and the student thinks something broke. Fix: always `git branch -D demo-agentic-coding` between runs (Dan does exactly this on camera at ~17:56).
- **Second stall:** running the programmable script from inside the `demo-agentic-coding` branch instead of `main` — teaches why runbooks state their starting state.
- **Cost anxiety:** each headless run is a small number of agent turns; the lab total is modest. If a student can't run it at all, the budget conversation (pay to play) is the actual lesson surfacing early.
- **What this lab intentionally does NOT cover:** skills, triggers, parallelism, CI embedding — later lessons. Deflect scope creep to keep the primitive crisp.
