1	# TAC-7 Lab Spec — ZTE: The Secret of Agentic Engineering
2	
3	**Scope rule:** every drill runs inside the course codebase only (`codebase/` → `tac/tac-7`; students: `git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-7.git`). You additionally need a GitHub repo **you control** — the ADW pipeline IS issues, comments, and PRs. No external repos, no new machinery; every workflow in tac-7 is already `_iso`.
4	**Prime directive (graded throughout):** you type **zero** lines of application code by hand, AND you record your **presence** honestly for every run (how many times you touched it: prompt only = 1, prompt + review = 2, anything more = you were in-loop). The point of this lab is to *watch your own presence fall per problem class* — not to reach ZTE on run one.
5	**Time box:** 2–3 hours (the capstone lab). Token cost is real and the highest of the course: multiple full plan→build→test→review→document runs, one on `model_set heavy` (opus), plus a ship. Budget for it; running out mid-ship and blaming ZTE is the failure the pay-to-play lesson is designed to surface.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## 0 · Setup (20 min)
10	
11	1. Clone the lesson repo: `git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-7.git && cd tac-7`. **Own the review surface:** create your own GitHub repo, `git remote remove origin && git remote add origin <your-repo> && git push -u origin main` (Dan does the equivalent on-video by resetting origin). `gh auth status` must be green.
12	2. Copy `.env.sample` → `.env`; set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (the headless billing path) and `export GITHUB_REPO_URL`. Fill `app/server/.env` for the NL→SQL app's own key. **Optional but demo-faithful:** the four Cloudflare R2 vars so review screenshots render as images on the issue — without them you get local file paths, and **that is not an error** (the uploader disables silently).
13	3. Verify the toolchain: `claude --version`, `gh auth status`, `uv --version`, `bun --version`, `git --version` (must support worktrees).
14	4. Boot the app once yourself: `./scripts/start.sh` → `http://localhost:5173`; upload sample data; run one NL query; `./scripts/stop_apps.sh`. You need to know what "working" looks like before an agent ships to it.
15	5. Read `.claude/settings.json` and `adws/README.md`. Say out loud, before you run anything: what may a workflow do, and where will its evidence land? *(Answer you're building toward: `agents/<adw_id>/` for state + logs, `trees/<adw_id>/` for the isolated app copy, and the issue thread for every human-visible report.)*
16	
17	**Checkpoint 0:** you can name the three places evidence lands and state why review/patch/ship need a repo you own — their output *is* issue comments, PR updates, and a merge.
18	
19	## 1 · One issue → a production-shaped run (30 min)
20	
21	1. File a GitHub issue in Dan's shape: `Add a footer showing the current table count. adw_sdlc_iso`. Run it manually first (webhook comes later): `cd adws && uv run adw_sdlc_iso.py <issue#>`. Hands off the repo the moment it starts.
22	2. While it runs, **prove the isolation with your own eyes:** `git worktree list` shows `trees/<adw_id>`; `cat trees/<adw_id>/.ports.env` shows the deterministic 9100-/9200-range pair; `cat agents/<adw_id>/adw_state.json` — name all **ten** fields aloud.
23	3. Jump into the agent's environment mid-run, like Dan: `code trees/<adw_id>` and watch the branch in the status bar. You are a guest in the agent's world, not a co-editor — do not touch files.
24	4. When it finishes, audit the evidence chain top-to-bottom on the issue: classification → state JSON → plan path → test summary → review summary **with ≥1 screenshot** → documentation → the PR. Open the PR diff.
25	
26	**Checkpoint 1:** the issue thread reads as a complete paper trail, and you can point at where each of the ten state fields got populated. Record your presence for this run.
27	
28	## 2 · Go in-loop on purpose (15 min)
29	
30	1. This is the beat most students skip. In `claude`, run `/in_loop_review <branch-name>`; it fetches + checks out the branch, resets/starts the app, and opens `localhost` for hands-on inspection.
31	2. Exercise the footer feature yourself in the browser. Write one sentence: **what did your review catch?** (Be honest — on a clean run, likely nothing.)
32	
33	**Checkpoint 2:** you can explain Dan's "in loop moving toward out loop" from experience — you *chose* to add a touchpoint, and you can say whether it added value. When it stops adding value for this class, that's the signal to drop it.
34	
35	## 3 · Turn the compute knob (20 min)
36	
37	1. New issue, heavier work: `Generate random rows for a selected table. adw_sdlc_iso model_set heavy`. Run it.
38	2. **Prove the knob actually turned:** find which model the implementor ran — `agents/<adw_id>/sdlc_implementor/raw_output.jsonl` (the `model` field) or the "Model Set" line in the issue thread. Confirm the implementor escalated to **opus** while classification/branch/test stayed on **sonnet**.
39	
40	**Checkpoint 3:** you can state that `model_set` is one IDK read by `/classify_adw`, stored in `adw_state.json`, and that exactly **8 of 18** commands escalate on heavy — and you have on-disk evidence that yours did.
41	
42	## 4 · Patch class vs full SDLC (15 min)
43	
44	1. Small, surgical change: `Rename the Query button to Run. adw_patch_iso`. Run it.
45	2. Compare its footprint to the full SDLC runs: the plan lives under `specs/patch/`, and only a subset of phases ran (worktree → targeted patch plan → implement → PR — no full plan/test/review/document ceremony).
46	
47	**Checkpoint 4 (one sentence):** why is the CSV/text-rename class routed to `patch` instead of `sdlc`? *(It's "just changing one thing" — a different composition of the same primitives, not a smaller SDLC. This is the secret in miniature.)*
48	
49	## 5 · The ZTE ceremony and the uppercase interlock (30 min)
50	
51	1. The low-stakes class ZTE is earned on first: `/chore adw_sdlc_ZTE_iso - change the background color to light green` (**ZTE uppercase**). Watch all six phases; note the initiation comment's auto-merge warning.
52	2. Confirm the merge landed **with no human step**: `git pull && git log --oneline -3` shows a merge commit `...via ADW Ship workflow`, and the app served from `main` shows the change.

**Time box:** 2–3 hours (the capstone lab). Token cost is real and the highest of the course: multiple full plan→build→test→review→document runs, one on `model_set heavy` (opus), plus a ship. ---

## 0 · Setup (20 min)

Clone the lesson repo: `git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-7.git && cd tac-7`. **Own the review surface:** create your own GitHub repo, `git remote remove origin && git remote add origin <your-repo> && git push -u origin main` (Dan does the equivalent on-video by resetting origin). `gh auth status` must be green.
2. Copy `.env.sample` → `.env`; set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (the headless billing path) and `export GITHUB_REPO_URL`. Fill `app/server/.env` for the NL→SQL app's own key. **Optional but demo-faithful:** the four Cloudflare R2 vars so review screenshots render as images on the issue — without them you get local file paths, and **that is not an error** (the uploader disables silently).
3. Verify the toolchain: `claude --version`, `gh auth status`, `uv --version`, `bun --version`, `git --version` (must support worktrees).
4. Boot the app once yourself: `./scripts/start.sh` → `http://localhost:5173`; upload sample data; run one NL query; `./scripts/stop_apps.sh`. You need to know what "working" looks like before an agent ships to it.
5. Read `.claude/settings.json` and `adws/README.md`. Say out loud, before you run anything: what may a workflow do, and where will its evidence land? *(Answer you're building toward: `agents/<adw_id>/` for state + logs, `trees/<adw_id>/` for the isolated app copy, and the issue thread for every human-visible report.)*

**Checkpoint 0:** you can name the three places evidence lands and state why review/patch/ship need a repo you own — their output *is* issue comments, PR updates, and a merge.

## 1 · One issue → a production-shaped run (30 min)

1. File a GitHub issue in Dan's shape: `Add a footer showing the current table count. adw_sdlc_iso`. Run it manually first (webhook comes later): `cd adws && uv run adw_sdlc_iso.py <issue#>`. Hands off the repo the moment it starts.

3. Jump into the agent's environment mid-run, like Dan: `code trees/<adw_id>` and watch the branch in the status bar. You are a guest in the agent's world, not a co-editor — do not touch files.
4. When it finishes, audit the evidence chain top-to-bottom on the issue: classification → state JSON → plan path → test summary → review summary **with ≥1 screenshot** → documentation → the PR. Open the PR diff.

**Checkpoint 1:** the issue thread reads as a complete paper trail, and you can point at where each of the ten state fields got populated. Record your presence for this run.

## 2 · Go in-loop on purpose (15 min)

1. This is the beat most students skip. In `claude`, run `/in_loop_review <branch-name>`; it fetches + checks out the branch, resets/starts the app, and opens `localhost` for hands-on inspection.
2. Exercise the footer feature yourself in the browser. Write one sentence: **what did your review catch?** (Be honest — on a clean run, likely nothing.)

1	# TAC-7 · ZTE Secret of Agentic Engineering — Master Teaching Notes
2	
3	**Tactic #7: Target Zero-Touch Engineering.** Video 53:20 (3200s), advanced, second-to-last lesson. Codebase `tac/tac-7` (loot box: `git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-7.git`) — the TAC-6 Natural Language SQL app wrapped in the finished agentic layer: 14 isolated ADW workflow scripts, 33 command prompts, worktree isolation, model sets, webhook + cron triggers, and the auto-shipping ZTE pipeline.
4	
5	The lesson runs in an unusual shape: first ~28 minutes are a *dividend-collection demo* (five real pieces of work handed to the layer and shipped in parallel while Dan reviews), then the *velocity-scale reveal* (in-loop → out-loop → ZTE), a live ZTE run that merges to main untouched, and finally the course's *secret*. Teach it in that order — evidence first, doctrine second.
6	
7	Teaching model per idea: **Hook → Picture → Worked example → Name (Dan's term) → Failure mode → Retrieval.**
8	
9	---
10	
11	## Idea 1 — Payday: five pieces of work, one engineer, zero typing
12	
13	- **Hook:** This morning you have three features, a chore, and a bug in your queue. Estimate honestly: a week? Dan files all five as GitHub issues in six minutes and goes to review something else. All five ship.
14	- **Picture:** Frame t0250 (4:10) — a GitHub "Create new issue" form. The body is plain English plus two keywords: `/feature`, `adw_sdlc_iso`. Then frame t0372 (6:12) — the webhook terminal detecting the event, initializing state, allocating ports 9106/9206.
15	- **Worked example:** #51 drop-zone surface area (feature), #52 JSON export (feature), table random data (feature, `model_set heavy`), #54 bump the NL→SQL model to o4-mini (chore), and a CSV-text bug routed to the lightweight patch workflow instead of full SDLC (5:22). "Five issues getting tackled by our agentic pipelines... all happening in parallel" (7:25). "This is absurd levels of scale" (7:08).
16	- **Name:** Collecting the dividends of the agentic layer. "Once you've built the system that builds the system, it's going to pay you back massively."
17	- **Failure mode:** Believing something new was built for this demo. It's TAC-4's PITER + TAC-5's loops + TAC-6's focused agents, *composed and run in parallel*. The delta of lesson 7 is scale and the removal of the last human step — not new machinery.
18	- **Retrieval:** Which of the five pieces of work did NOT get the full SDLC, and what got it instead? *(The CSV-text bug → adw_patch_iso, a targeted patch plan + implement + PR.)*
19	
20	## Idea 2 — The Agentic Engineering Velocity Scale (the lesson's spine)
21	
22	- **Hook:** How present are you in your own engineering? Score yourself: driving every prompt (always present), showing up twice (prompt, review), or once (prompt only)?
23	- **Picture:** Frame t0100 (1:40) — the on-screen scale: **1 In-Loop → 2 Out-Loop → 3 ZTE**.
24	- **Worked example:** The whole lesson walks the scale left to right: interactive `claude` sessions (in-loop, the clone-and-/install ritual at 8:15), the five-issue parallel run (out-loop, presence two: Dan prompts, then reviews), and issue #62 (ZTE, presence one: prompt → production).
25	- **Name:** "There are three levels: in loop, out loop, and one additional level..." (1:28). Presence numbers from the course card: out-loop = two touchpoints, ZTE = one.
26	- **Failure mode:** Reading the scale as a switch. Dan's own words: "It's not in loop versus out loop. It's in loop moving toward out loop" (9:42) — and he *deliberately* goes back in-loop at 22:59 to hand-review the drag-and-drop PR. Progress is per-problem-class, "one day at a time."
27	- **Retrieval:** Name the three levels and your presence count at each. *(In-loop/continuous; out-loop/2; ZTE/1.)*
28	
29	## Idea 3 — Git worktrees: N agents, one device, zero collisions
30	
31	- **Hook:** Fire two agents in the same repo directory and watch them fight over the same branch, dev server, and database. Now fire five without a fight.
32	- **Picture:** Frame t0680 (11:20) — `trees/` expanded to a dozen 8-hex-char directories, each a *complete copy of the application* owned by one agent. Frame t0890 (14:50) — the state file that remembers which copy belongs to whom.
33	- **Worked example:** `adw_plan_iso.py` creates `trees/<adw_id>/` via `git worktree add -b <branch> ... origin/main`, allocates deterministic ports (base-36 hash of the ADW ID % 15 → backend 9100–9114, frontend 9200–9214, socket-checked with fallback), writes `.ports.env`, then runs `/install_worktree` *inside the worktree*: copy `.env`s, append ports, copy `.mcp.json` + Playwright config and rewrite paths to absolute, `uv sync`, `bun install`, reset the DB. At 12:58 Dan jumps into a live one: `code trees/<id>` — branch `chore-...-issue-39-...` in the status bar.
34	- **Name:** Isolated ADWs (`_iso` suffix — every workflow in tac-7 is iso). "In every tree, the application exists for a specific agent to build in. This is the easiest way to parallelize your workflows" (11:17).
35	- **Failure mode:** Worktree fixation. Dan pre-empts it twice: "It doesn't matter that you use Git work trees... Docker... I don't care how you scale up your agent environments, it only matters that you can" (~11:40). (The repo even ships an E2B cloud-sandbox PoC in `adws/adw_tests/sandbox_poc.py`.) Second failure: never running `scripts/purge_tree.sh` and discovering each worktree is a full repo copy the hard way.
36	- **Retrieval:** An ADW ID hashes to index 7. Which two ports does the run get, and what file records them? *(9107 and 9207 — `.ports.env` in the worktree, mirrored into `adw_state.json`.)*
37	
38	## Idea 4 — The state object: pipeline memory outside the context window
39	
40	- **Hook:** Phase 2 of your pipeline needs the branch name phase 1 created. Where does it live — in a prompt? In your head?
41	- **Picture:** Frame t0890 — `agents/e2ae7fad/adw_state.json` open in the editor: ten fields, every one load-bearing.
42	- **Worked example:** `adw_id, issue_number, branch_name, plan_file, issue_class, worktree_path, backend_port, frontend_port, model_set, all_adws`. Every phase does load → contribute → save. `all_adws` appends each workflow that ran (that's how KPI "attempts" is computed later). And `adw_ship_iso` turns state into a gate: all eight required fields non-null or no merge.
43	- **Name:** The ADW state object. "Expect to have to add some type of state object inside your dedicated agent environments... it frees your agent to do one thing extraordinarily well... and lets you jump in and replay what that agent has done" (14:55–15:06).
44	- **Failure mode:** Stuffing pipeline bookkeeping into the agent's context instead — which breaks TAC-6's one-agent-one-prompt-one-purpose ("has not been broken. This is really important for scaling," 14:29) and makes runs unreplayable.
45	- **Retrieval:** Ship aborts with "missing fields." Which mechanism caught it, and what does that tell you about the run? *(State-completeness validation — some phase never ran/never saved; the paper trail says which.)*
46	
47	## Idea 5 — Model sets: compute allocation as one information-dense keyword
48	
49	- **Hook:** One of your five issues is a big feature; another is a text rename. Should both burn your most expensive model?
50	- **Picture:** Frame t1010 (16:50) — `agents.py`'s `SLASH_COMMAND_MODEL_MAP` on screen: eighteen commands, each mapped for `base` and `heavy`.
51	- **Worked example:** Typing `model_set heavy` in the issue → `/classify_adw` parses it into state → every `execute_template` call resolves its model from the map. On heavy, exactly 8 commands escalate sonnet→opus (`/implement`, `/resolve_failed_test`, `/resolve_failed_e2e_test`, `/document`, `/chore`, `/bug`, `/feature`, `/patch`); classification, branch naming, test, review, commit, PR stay sonnet. Inside the prompts, "think hard" IDKs activate reasoning (17:25). The heavy random-data feature runs 27 minutes on opus and ships ~300 lines.
52	- **Name:** Model sets — "a knob to turn to increase the compute that our workflow uses" (16:45); IDK = information-dense keyword (from TAC-2/AH vocabulary): "You can encode any information dense keyword you want. You just have to make sure that your prompts recognize it and pick it up" (16:04).
53	- **Failure mode:** `model_set heavy` on everything "to be safe" — paying opus prices for JSON extraction. The map's selectivity IS the lesson: compute allocation is an engineering decision you encode once, then invoke with one word.
54	- **Retrieval:** Which phase reads `model_set` off the raw issue text, and where is the value stored so later phases agree? *(/classify_adw at trigger time; persisted in adw_state.json.)*
55	
56	## Idea 6 — Review = proof of value (and the trigger for everything after)
57	
58	- **Hook:** Your agent says "done." Your PM asks "is it though?" What arrives in your review system without you lifting a finger?
59	- **Picture:** Frame t1290 (21:30) — issue #51's thread: "📷 Screenshots — Captured 4 screenshots," the app visible with the new drop overlay.
60	- **Worked example:** The review agent boots the app *in the worktree on its own ports*, drives it with Playwright MCP, takes 1–5 numbered screenshots of critical paths only, classifies findings (`skippable` / `tech_debt` / `blocker` — success means *no blockers*), returns strict JSON, uploads images to Cloudflare R2, posts them to the issue. Blockers aren't just reported: the review workflow patches and re-reviews ("attempt 1/3" visible on #54's thread). Dan: "Our agents took images and gave us proof that the feature has shipped" (21:26). The named next step: video — "have your agents take video, upload it to a cloud bucket, and post the URLs" (26:12); the Playwright config already records 1920×1080 video per run.
61	- **Name:** Proof of value. "It's not 'does it work?' It's 'is what we built what we asked for?'" (21:40) — TAC-5's review question, now automated end-to-end. "Having a comprehensive review system is a massive, massive edge" (and "an entire product category," 25:40).
62	- **Failure mode:** Never opening the screenshots. The review system is how trust gets *earned*; skip it and your presence never legitimately drops. Opposite failure: treating review as re-testing — tests already gated the pipeline; review compares to the SPEC.
63	- **Retrieval:** Three severity levels, and which one flips `success` to false? *(skippable, tech_debt, blocker — only blocker.)*
64	
65	## Idea 7 — The realization: your review is the bottleneck (KPIs prove it)
66	
67	- **Hook:** Tenth time this month your pipeline shipped a chore flawlessly. You reviewed all ten. What did review #10 contribute? Be honest: latency.
68	- **Picture:** No frame — this beat is spoken over B-roll (render as a designed pull-quote). The instrument is `app_docs/agentic_kpis.md`: attempts, plan size, diff size, presence, streak.
69	- **Worked example:** The committed KPI table is a real run's receipt: ADW `cc73faf1`, issue #47, `/chore`, attempts 1, plan 39 lines, diff 274/5/10, average presence 1.0, streak 1 — a ZTE run whose committed spec still carries the trigger text `/chore adw_sdlc_ZTE_iso - update 'Upload Data' to be 'Upload'`. The KPI command recomputes streak/attempts with forced `python -c` arithmetic inside the document phase.
70	- **Name:** The bottleneck realization: "This human in the loop model is a bottleneck. I'm not catching any bugs anymore. I'm not adding any value outside of the agentic layer. I'm going to remove the human in the loop review process *for this class of problems*" (30:45). Foreshadowed at 2:06: "a bottleneck, not a safety net."
71	- **Failure mode:** Making the call on vibes in either direction — YOLO-merging without a streak, or refusing forever despite one. The KPIs exist precisely so this is an *evidence-gated* decision per problem class ("90% of the time there's no issues, and that number keeps going up," 39:52–40:06).
72	- **Retrieval:** Which KPI directly encodes "how touched" a run was, and what value does ZTE target? *(Presence; 1.)*

74	## Idea 8 — Tactic #7: Target Zero-Touch Engineering (PITER → PITE)

76	- **Hook:** TAC-1 told you to stop coding and you (eventually) did. The same argument now comes for the thing you replaced coding with: reviewing.
77	- **Picture:** Frame t1912 (31:52) — the course tactic card: definition (presence KPI 2 → 1) + daily actions, including "Go from PITER to PITE with one prompt agentic workflows."

Just like you've stopped coding, you'll stop reviewing" (31:33–31:46) → "This is the lesson seven tactic: Target zero touch engineering... the ultimate agentic coding North Star" (31:50) → KPI shape: "Attempts at one, size constantly scaling up, streak constantly increasing... drop your presence down to one" (31:56).
79	- **Name:** Zero-Touch Engineering (tactic; the *code* calls it Zero Touch Execution — same acronym, both appear in course artifacts). The word **Target** in the tactic name is load-bearing: it's a North Star, not a day-one state.
80	- **Failure mode:** The O-face objection, named in-lesson (32:37): "this isn't a real production application, you're pushing way too far." Dan agrees the app is a toy and redirects: start with chores → bugs → features (33:07); the tactic is *targeting* ZTE so you discover when it's real for each class — "how else will you know unless you're trying?" (37:25).
81	- **Retrieval:** What does PITER lose under ZTE, and what replaces it? *(The R/review; it's replaced by embedded pipeline gates — tests, agentic review with proof, state validation — not by nothing.)*

83	## Idea 9 — The ZTE pipeline in code: gates, ship mechanics, and one uppercase interlock
84	
85	- **Hook:** "Agents auto-merging to main" sounds like a horror story. Read the 240 lines of `adw_sdlc_zte_iso.py` and count the ways it refuses to.

Gates in source: test failure → "ZTE Aborted"; review failure → "ZTE Aborted"; documentation failure → warn but continue ("shouldn't block shipping"); ship failure → report + manual-merge advice. Ship itself: validate all 8 state fields → validate worktree (state + filesystem + `git worktree list`) → in the repo root: fetch, checkout main, pull, `git merge --no-ff` (message "Merge branch '<branch>' via ADW Ship workflow"), push origin main — restoring the original branch on every failure path. Upstream, the interlock: `/classify_adw` refuses `adw_sdlc_ZTE_iso` unless **ZTE is explicitly uppercase**; lowercase silently downgrades to reviewed SDLC. Also verified: both SDLC orchestrators hardcode `--skip-e2e` — unit tests gate the pipeline, browser E2E is a separate standalone run.
88	- **Name:** Zero Touch Execution workflow; the ship phase; "our final approval step" (state validation, per the docstring).
89	- **Failure mode (three, all real):** (1) assuming E2E ran — it didn't; (2) trusting `adws/README.md`'s "approves the PR, squash method" — the code does a manual `--no-ff` merge + push (Dan's narration at 33:55 matches the code, the README is stale — verify countable claims against source); (3) typing lowercase `zte` and mistaking the working interlock for a bug.
90	- **Retrieval:** Which failing phase does NOT stop a ZTE run, and which check runs before any git command in ship? *(Documentation; the 8-field state completeness check + worktree validation.)*

93	
94	- **Hook:** What does presence-of-one actually look like on a Tuesday?
95	- **Picture:** Frame t2958 (49:18) — the app after `git pull origin main`, wearing the background color an agent shipped. Review evidence earlier: "Background is green" screenshots in the review step (44:16).
96	- **Worked example:** Issue #62 "Update the background color" with `/chore adw_sdlc_ZTE_iso` (34:38–34:58) → initiation (35:31) → plan/build/test/review/document on base models → auto-merge → "It's deployed to production. The issue is closed. All I did was write this prompt" (48:31). Dan's framing of the class: designer-whim styling changes — "this is not something you should ever spend your time on... low hanging fruit" (34:20).
97	- **Name:** "This is zero touch engineering. This is the future of engineering" (49:20). Prod here = main branch; "for you, this will be your deploy — staging, production, however your engineering is configured" (44:50).

99	- **Retrieval:** In tac-7, what concretely is "production," and where does Dan say your version of ship should point? *(Push to main; your deploy pipeline/staging/prod.)*

101	## Idea 11 — The secret: composable agentic primitives (SDLC demoted)
102	
103	- **Hook:** Seven lessons of plan → build → test → review → document. Now the instructor tells you the SDLC was never the point. Why isn't that a rug-pull?
104	- **Picture:** Frame t2765 (46:05) — "The Secret: Composable Agentic Primitives": Agentic Primitives (ADWs, Templates, Plans, Architecture, Tests, Documentation, Types, Standard Out, Tools, Prompt, Model, Context) → ADW steps (Plan/Build/Test/Review/Document/Deploy) → Composed Workflows (Plan→Build→Test, Build→Review→Deploy, Test→Document, **ANY WORKFLOW**).
105	- **Worked example:** The repo already practices the secret: 14 workflow scripts are *arrangements* of the same phase modules — plan_build, plan_build_test, plan_build_review, plan_build_test_review, plan_build_document, sdlc, sdlc_zte, patch, ship — and the CSV bug took a different composition (patch) than the features (sdlc) on the same infrastructure.
106	- **Name:** Stated twice, verbatim (45:58–46:10): "The secret of tactical agentic coding is that it's not about the software developer lifecycle at all. It's about composable agentic primitives you can use to solve any engineering problem class." SDLC: "powerful, but... a remnant of the past" (46:26); "this arrangement of ADWs is completely arbitrary... The one way is the way that ships in your codebase" (47:20).
107	- **Failure mode:** Hearing "SDLC is dead, delete my pipeline." The SDLC "still works, it's still very relevant... a package for me to deliver a message" — the failure is enshrining ANY fixed arrangement instead of owning the primitives and recomposing per problem class ("it's going to look a bit different for every single organization").
108	- **Retrieval:** Give the secret in one sentence, and name four primitives from the slide. *(Not the SDLC — composable agentic primitives for any problem class; e.g. templates, plans, prompts, ADWs.)*
109	
110	## Idea 12 — Belief, the four postures, and the closing arc
111	
112	- **Hook:** Everything in this lesson is copy-able this weekend. Dan says the real blocker isn't technical. What is it?
113	- **Picture:** No frame — the futures monologue (38:55–39:20) plays over B-roll; render the four postures as a designed diagram: run away / stand still / move toward / **sprint**.
114	- **Worked example:** The two-engineer comparison (39:30–40:40): a few weeks of agentic-layer investment → "write a single prompt, hit enter, ship into production... 90% of the time no issues, and that number keeps going up — every tool release, every model release." Versus: open Jira, prompt in-loop, sit, wait, iterate, retest. "Tell me who wins this. Tell me who makes their business more money" (40:36).
115	- **Name:** "The real challenge... is about your belief. You have to believe that the agentic layer is worth investing into... If you don't believe that your agents can run your codebase, you're cooked" (41:10–41:18). "It's not about being right. It's about being prepared to win" (41:35). Career close: "you'll be the engineer they can't replace... because you understand and control the agentic layer... the area of highest leverage" (44:00→49:44: "1x input becomes 10x output, 10x becomes 100x").
116	- **Failure mode:** Consuming the monologue as motivation-content and changing nothing. The lesson's own ask is one concrete step: pick a chore class this week, encode it, instrument it, let the KPIs argue.
117	- **Retrieval:** The arc in one line: what did TAC-1 remove, what does TAC-7 remove, and what number tracks both? *(Typing, then reviewing; presence.)*

# TAC-7 · ZTE Secret of Agentic Engineering — Master Teaching Notes

**Tactic #7: Target Zero-Touch Engineering.** Video 53:20 (3200s), advanced, second-to-last lesson. Codebase `tac/tac-7` (loot box: `git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-7.git`) — the TAC-6 Natural Language SQL app wrapped in the finished agentic layer: 14 isolated ADW workflow scripts, 33 command prompts, worktree isolation, model sets, webhook + cron triggers, and the auto-shipping ZTE pipeline.

The lesson runs in an unusual shape: first ~28 minutes are a *dividend-collection demo* (five real pieces of work handed to the layer and shipped in parallel while Dan reviews), then the *velocity-scale reveal* (in-loop → out-loop → ZTE), a live ZTE run that merges to main untouched, and finally the course's *secret*. Teach it in that order — evidence first, doctrine second.

Teaching model per idea: **Hook → Picture → Worked example → Name (Dan's term) → Failure mode → Retrieval.**

---

## Idea 1 — Payday: five pieces of work, one engineer, zero typing

- **Hook:** This morning you have three features, a chore, and a bug in your queue. Estimate honestly: a week? Dan files all five as GitHub issues in six minutes and goes to review something else. All five ship.
- **Picture:** Frame t0250 (4:10) — a GitHub "Create new issue" form. The body is plain English plus two keywords: `/feature`, `adw_sdlc_iso`. Then frame t0372 (6:12) — the webhook terminal detecting the event, initializing state, allocating ports 9106/9206.
- **Worked example:** #51 drop-zone surface area (feature), #52 JSON export (feature), table random data (feature, `model_set heavy`), #54 bump the NL→SQL model to o4-mini (chore), and a CSV-text bug routed to the lightweight patch workflow instead of full SDLC (5:22). "Five issues getting tackled by our agentic pipelines... all happening in parallel" (7:25). "This is absurd levels of scale" (7:08).
- **Name:** Collecting the dividends of the agentic layer. "Once you've built the system that builds the system, it's going to pay you back massively."
- **Failure mode:** Believing something new was built for this demo. It's TAC-4's PITER + TAC-5's loops + TAC-6's focused agents, *composed and run in parallel*. The delta of lesson 7 is scale and the removal of the last human step — not new machinery.
- **Retrieval:** Which of the five pieces of work did NOT get the full SDLC, and what got it instead? *(The CSV-text bug → adw_patch_iso, a targeted patch plan + implement + PR.)*

## Idea 2 — The Agentic Engineering Velocity Scale (the lesson's spine)

- **Hook:** How present are you in your own engineering? Score yourself: driving every prompt (always present), showing up twice (prompt, review), or once (prompt only)?
- **Picture:** Frame t0100 (1:40) — the on-screen scale: **1 In-Loop → 2 Out-Loop → 3 ZTE**.
- **Worked example:** The whole lesson walks the scale left to right: interactive `claude` sessions (in-loop, the clone-and-/install ritual at 8:15), the five-issue parallel run (out-loop, presence two: Dan prompts, then reviews), and issue #62 (ZTE, presence one: prompt → production).
- **Name:** "There are three levels: in loop, out loop, and one additional level..." (1:28). Presence numbers from the course card: out-loop = two touchpoints, ZTE = one.
- **Failure mode:** Reading the scale as a switch. Dan's own words: "It's not in loop versus out loop. It's in loop moving toward out loop" (9:42) — and he *deliberately* goes back in-loop at 22:59 to hand-review the drag-and-drop PR. Progress is per-problem-class, "one day at a time."
- **Retrieval:** Name the three levels and your presence count at each. *(In-loop/continuous; out-loop/2; ZTE/1.)*

## Idea 3 — Git worktrees: N agents, one device, zero collisions

- **Hook:** Fire two agents in the same repo directory and watch them fight over the same branch, dev server, and database. Now fire five without a fight.
- **Picture:** Frame t0680 (11:20) — `trees/` expanded to a dozen 8-hex-char directories, each a *complete copy of the application* owned by one agent. Frame t0890 (14:50) — the state file that remembers which copy belongs to whom.
- **Worked example:** `adw_plan_iso.py` creates `trees/<adw_id>/` via `git worktree add -b <branch> ... origin/main`, allocates deterministic ports (base-36 hash of the ADW ID % 15 → backend 9100–9114, frontend 9200–9214, socket-checked with fallback), writes `.ports.env`, then runs `/install_worktree` *inside the worktree*: copy `.env`s, append ports, copy `.mcp.json` + Playwright config and rewrite paths to absolute, `uv sync`, `bun install`, reset the DB. At 12:58 Dan jumps into a live one: `code trees/<id>` — branch `chore-...-issue-39-...` in the status bar.
- **Name:** Isolated ADWs (`_iso` suffix — every workflow in tac-7 is iso). "In every tree, the application exists for a specific agent to build in. This is the easiest way to parallelize your workflows" (11:17).
- **Failure mode:** Worktree fixation. Dan pre-empts it twice: "It doesn't matter that you use Git work trees... Docker... I don't care how you scale up your agent environments, it only matters that you can" (~11:40). (The repo even ships an E2B cloud-sandbox PoC in `adws/adw_tests/sandbox_poc.py`.) Second failure: never running `scripts/purge_tree.sh` and discovering each worktree is a full repo copy the hard way.
- **Retrieval:** An ADW ID hashes to index 7. Which two ports does the run get, and what file records them? *(9107 and 9207 — `.ports.env` in the worktree, mirrored into `adw_state.json`.)*

## Idea 4 — The state object: pipeline memory outside the context window

- **Hook:** Phase 2 of your pipeline needs the branch name phase 1 created. Where does it live — in a prompt? In your head?
- **Picture:** Frame t0890 — `agents/e2ae7fad/adw_state.json` open in the editor: ten fields, every one load-bearing.
- **Worked example:** `adw_id, issue_number, branch_name, plan_file, issue_class, worktree_path, backend_port, frontend_port, model_set, all_adws`. Every phase does load → contribute → save. `all_adws` appends each workflow that ran (that's how KPI "attempts" is computed later). And `adw_ship_iso` turns state into a gate: all eight required fields non-null or no merge.
- **Name:** The ADW state object. "Expect to have to add some type of state object inside your dedicated agent environments... it frees your agent to do one thing extraordinarily well... and lets you jump in and replay what that agent has done" (14:55–15:06).
- **Failure mode:** Stuffing pipeline bookkeeping into the agent's context instead — which breaks TAC-6's one-agent-one-prompt-one-purpose ("has not been broken. This is really important for scaling," 14:29) and makes runs unreplayable.
- **Retrieval:** Ship aborts with "missing fields." Which mechanism caught it, and what does that tell you about the run? *(State-completeness validation — some phase never ran/never saved; the paper trail says which.)*

## Idea 5 — Model sets: compute allocation as one information-dense keyword

- **Hook:** One of your five issues is a big feature; another is a text rename. Should both burn your most expensive model?
- **Picture:** Frame t1010 (16:50) — `agents.py`'s `SLASH_COMMAND_MODEL_MAP` on screen: eighteen commands, each mapped for `base` and `heavy`.
- **Worked example:** Typing `model_set heavy` in the issue → `/classify_adw` parses it into state → every `execute_template` call resolves its model from the map. On heavy, exactly 8 commands escalate sonnet→opus (`/implement`, `/resolve_failed_test`, `/resolve_failed_e2e_test`, `/document`, `/chore`, `/bug`, `/feature`, `/patch`); classification, branch naming, test, review, commit, PR stay sonnet. Inside the prompts, "think hard" IDKs activate reasoning (17:25). The heavy random-data feature runs 27 minutes on opus and ships ~300 lines.
- **Name:** Model sets — "a knob to turn to increase the compute that our workflow uses" (16:45); IDK = information-dense keyword (from TAC-2/AH vocabulary): "You can encode any information dense keyword you want. You just have to make sure that your prompts recognize it and pick it up" (16:04).
- **Failure mode:** `model_set heavy` on everything "to be safe" — paying opus prices for JSON extraction. The map's selectivity IS the lesson: compute allocation is an engineering decision you encode once, then invoke with one word.
- **Retrieval:** Which phase reads `model_set` off the raw issue text, and where is the value stored so later phases agree? *(/classify_adw at trigger time; persisted in adw_state.json.)*

## Idea 6 — Review = proof of value (and the trigger for everything after)

- **Hook:** Your agent says "done." Your PM asks "is it though?" What arrives in your review system without you lifting a finger?
- **Picture:** Frame t1290 (21:30) — issue #51's thread: "📷 Screenshots — Captured 4 screenshots," the app visible with the new drop overlay.
- **Worked example:** The review agent boots the app *in the worktree on its own ports*, drives it with Playwright MCP, takes 1–5 numbered screenshots of critical paths only, classifies findings (`skippable` / `tech_debt` / `blocker` — success means *no blockers*), returns strict JSON, uploads images to Cloudflare R2, posts them to the issue. Blockers aren't just reported: the review workflow patches and re-reviews ("attempt 1/3" visible on #54's thread). Dan: "Our agents took images and gave us proof that the feature has shipped" (21:26). The named next step: video — "have your agents take video, upload it to a cloud bucket, and post the URLs" (26:12); the Playwright config already records 1920×1080 video per run.
- **Name:** Proof of value. "It's not 'does it work?' It's 'is what we built what we asked for?'" (21:40) — TAC-5's review question, now automated end-to-end. "Having a comprehensive review system is a massive, massive edge" (and "an entire product category," 25:40).
- **Failure mode:** Never opening the screenshots. The review system is how trust gets *earned*; skip it and your presence never legitimately drops. Opposite failure: treating review as re-testing — tests already gated the pipeline; review compares to the SPEC.
- **Retrieval:** Three severity levels, and which one flips `success` to false? *(skippable, tech_debt, blocker — only blocker.)*

## Idea 7 — The realization: your review is the bottleneck (KPIs prove it)

- **Hook:** Tenth time this month your pipeline shipped a chore flawlessly. You reviewed all ten. What did review #10 contribute? Be honest: latency.
- **Picture:** No frame — this beat is spoken over B-roll (render as a designed pull-quote). The instrument is `app_docs/agentic_kpis.md`: attempts, plan size, diff size, presence, streak.
- **Worked example:** The committed KPI table is a real run's receipt: ADW `cc73faf1`, issue #47, `/chore`, attempts 1, plan 39 lines, diff 274/5/10, average presence 1.0, streak 1 — a ZTE run whose committed spec still carries the trigger text `/chore adw_sdlc_ZTE_iso - update 'Upload Data' to be 'Upload'`. The KPI command recomputes streak/attempts with forced `python -c` arithmetic inside the document phase.
- **Name:** The bottleneck realization: "This human in the loop model is a bottleneck. I'm not catching any bugs anymore. I'm not adding any value outside of the agentic layer. I'm going to remove the human in the loop review process *for this class of problems*" (30:45). Foreshadowed at 2:06: "a bottleneck, not a safety net."
- **Failure mode:** Making the call on vibes in either direction — YOLO-merging without a streak, or refusing forever despite one. The KPIs exist precisely so this is an *evidence-gated* decision per problem class ("90% of the time there's no issues, and that number keeps going up," 39:52–40:06).
- **Retrieval:** Which KPI directly encodes "how touched" a run was, and what value does ZTE target? *(Presence; 1.)*

## Idea 8 — Tactic #7: Target Zero-Touch Engineering (PITER → PITE)

- **Hook:** TAC-1 told you to stop coding and you (eventually) did. The same argument now comes for the thing you replaced coding with: reviewing.
- **Picture:** Frame t1912 (31:52) — the course tactic card: definition (presence KPI 2 → 1) + daily actions, including "Go from PITER to PITE with one prompt agentic workflows."
- **Worked example:** The reveal sequence 30:45–32:30: bottleneck realization → "you'll drop yourself off the end of the out-loop PITER framework and it becomes PITE, not PITER. You'll drop off the review" (31:19) → "YOLO mode for your AI developer workflows... maximum confidence mode... Just like you've stopped coding, you'll stop reviewing" (31:33–31:46) → "This is the lesson seven tactic: Target zero touch engineering... the ultimate agentic coding North Star" (31:50) → KPI shape: "Attempts at one, size constantly scaling up, streak constantly increasing... drop your presence down to one" (31:56).
- **Name:** Zero-Touch Engineering (tactic; the *code* calls it Zero Touch Execution — same acronym, both appear in course artifacts). The word **Target** in the tactic name is load-bearing: it's a North Star, not a day-one state.
- **Failure mode:** The O-face objection, named in-lesson (32:37): "this isn't a real production application, you're pushing way too far." Dan agrees the app is a toy and redirects: start with chores → bugs → features (33:07); the tactic is *targeting* ZTE so you discover when it's real for each class — "how else will you know unless you're trying?" (37:25).
- **Retrieval:** What does PITER lose under ZTE, and what replaces it? *(The R/review; it's replaced by embedded pipeline gates — tests, agentic review with proof, state validation — not by nothing.)*

## Idea 9 — The ZTE pipeline in code: gates, ship mechanics, and one uppercase interlock

- **Hook:** "Agents auto-merging to main" sounds like a horror story. Read the 240 lines of `adw_sdlc_zte_iso.py` and count the ways it refuses to.
- **Picture:** Frame t2135 (35:35) — issue #62's initiation comment: six phases ending "🚢 Ship to production (approve & merge PR)" + "⚠️ Code will be automatically merged if all phases pass!"
- **Worked example:** ZTE = SDLC + ship. Gates in source: test failure → "ZTE Aborted"; review failure → "ZTE Aborted"; documentation failure → warn but continue ("shouldn't block shipping"); ship failure → report + manual-merge advice. Ship itself: validate all 8 state fields → validate worktree (state + filesystem + `git worktree list`) → in the repo root: fetch, checkout main, pull, `git merge --no-ff` (message "Merge branch '<branch>' via ADW Ship workflow"), push origin main — restoring the original branch on every failure path. Upstream, the interlock: `/classify_adw` refuses `adw_sdlc_ZTE_iso` unless **ZTE is explicitly uppercase**; lowercase silently downgrades to reviewed SDLC. Also verified: both SDLC orchestrators hardcode `--skip-e2e` — unit tests gate the pipeline, browser E2E is a separate standalone run.
- **Name:** Zero Touch Execution workflow; the ship phase; "our final approval step" (state validation, per the docstring).
- **Failure mode (three, all real):** (1) assuming E2E ran — it didn't; (2) trusting `adws/README.md`'s "approves the PR, squash method" — the code does a manual `--no-ff` merge + push (Dan's narration at 33:55 matches the code, the README is stale — verify countable claims against source); (3) typing lowercase `zte` and mistaking the working interlock for a bug.
- **Retrieval:** Which failing phase does NOT stop a ZTE run, and which check runs before any git command in ship? *(Documentation; the 8-field state completeness check + worktree validation.)*

## Idea 10 — The demo lands: one prompt to production

- **Hook:** What does presence-of-one actually look like on a Tuesday?
- **Picture:** Frame t2958 (49:18) — the app after `git pull origin main`, wearing the background color an agent shipped. Review evidence earlier: "Background is green" screenshots in the review step (44:16).
- **Worked example:** Issue #62 "Update the background color" with `/chore adw_sdlc_ZTE_iso` (34:38–34:58) → initiation (35:31) → plan/build/test/review/document on base models → auto-merge → "It's deployed to production. The issue is closed. All I did was write this prompt" (48:31). Dan's framing of the class: designer-whim styling changes — "this is not something you should ever spend your time on... low hanging fruit" (34:20).
- **Name:** "This is zero touch engineering. This is the future of engineering" (49:20). Prod here = main branch; "for you, this will be your deploy — staging, production, however your engineering is configured" (44:50).
- **Failure mode:** Scoffing at the example's size. The size is the point — ZTE is earned on exactly this class first. The committed repo carries the same class shipped for real (background: off-white → light-sky-blue `#E0F6FF`; button text "Upload Data" → "Upload").
- **Retrieval:** In tac-7, what concretely is "production," and where does Dan say your version of ship should point? *(Push to main; your deploy pipeline/staging/prod.)*

## Idea 11 — The secret: composable agentic primitives (SDLC demoted)

- **Hook:** Seven lessons of plan → build → test → review → document. Now the instructor tells you the SDLC was never the point. Why isn't that a rug-pull?
- **Picture:** Frame t2765 (46:05) — "The Secret: Composable Agentic Primitives": Agentic Primitives (ADWs, Templates, Plans, Architecture, Tests, Documentation, Types, Standard Out, Tools, Prompt, Model, Context) → ADW steps (Plan/Build/Test/Review/Document/Deploy) → Composed Workflows (Plan→Build→Test, Build→Review→Deploy, Test→Document, **ANY WORKFLOW**).
- **Worked example:** The repo already practices the secret: 14 workflow scripts are *arrangements* of the same phase modules — plan_build, plan_build_test, plan_build_review, plan_build_test_review, plan_build_document, sdlc, sdlc_zte, patch, ship — and the CSV bug took a different composition (patch) than the features (sdlc) on the same infrastructure.
- **Name:** Stated twice, verbatim (45:58–46:10): "The secret of tactical agentic coding is that it's not about the software developer lifecycle at all. It's about composable agentic primitives you can use to solve any engineering problem class." SDLC: "powerful, but... a remnant of the past" (46:26); "this arrangement of ADWs is completely arbitrary... The one way is the way that ships in your codebase" (47:20).
- **Failure mode:** Hearing "SDLC is dead, delete my pipeline." The SDLC "still works, it's still very relevant... a package for me to deliver a message" — the failure is enshrining ANY fixed arrangement instead of owning the primitives and recomposing per problem class ("it's going to look a bit different for every single organization").
- **Retrieval:** Give the secret in one sentence, and name four primitives from the slide. *(Not the SDLC — composable agentic primitives for any problem class; e.g. templates, plans, prompts, ADWs.)*

## Idea 12 — Belief, the four postures, and the closing arc

- **Hook:** Everything in this lesson is copy-able this weekend. Dan says the real blocker isn't technical. What is it?
- **Picture:** No frame — the futures monologue (38:55–39:20) plays over B-roll; render the four postures as a designed diagram: run away / stand still / move toward / **sprint**.
- **Worked example:** The two-engineer comparison (39:30–40:40): a few weeks of agentic-layer investment → "write a single prompt, hit enter, ship into production... 90% of the time no issues, and that number keeps going up — every tool release, every model release." Versus: open Jira, prompt in-loop, sit, wait, iterate, retest. "Tell me who wins this. Tell me who makes their business more money" (40:36).
- **Name:** "The real challenge... is about your belief. You have to believe that the agentic layer is worth investing into... If you don't believe that your agents can run your codebase, you're cooked" (41:10–41:18). "It's not about being right. It's about being prepared to win" (41:35). Career close: "you'll be the engineer they can't replace... because you understand and control the agentic layer... the area of highest leverage" (44:00→49:44: "1x input becomes 10x output, 10x becomes 100x").
- **Failure mode:** Consuming the monologue as motivation-content and changing nothing. The lesson's own ask is one concrete step: pick a chore class this week, encode it, instrument it, let the KPIs argue.
- **Retrieval:** The arc in one line: what did TAC-1 remove, what does TAC-7 remove, and what number tracks both? *(Typing, then reviewing; presence.)*

## Terminology glossary (canonical spellings; transcript mishears in parens)

- **ZTE** — Zero-Touch Engineering (tactic) / Zero Touch Execution (code & bot comments). Level 3 of the scale.
- **Agentic Engineering Velocity Scale** — In-Loop (1) → Out-Loop (2) → ZTE (3).
- **Presence** — KPI: how many touchpoints you have per shipped unit. Out-loop best = 2 (prompt, review); ZTE = 1.
- **PITER → PITE** ("Peter → Pete") — Prompt input, Trigger, Environment, Review; ZTE drops the R.
- **ADW** — AI Developer Workflow; `adws/` is "a scripting layer that lets us construct pipelines of agents that solve specific classes of problems back to back to back."
- **_iso** — isolated: the workflow runs in its own git worktree with dedicated ports.
- **Worktree / trees/<adw_id>** — full repo copy per run; ports 9100–9114 / 9200–9214 (15 slots).
- **ADW state object** — `agents/<adw_id>/adw_state.json`, ten fields, pipeline memory + ship gate.
- **Model set** ("model set heavy") — base|heavy IDK re-mapping each slash command's model; heavy→opus for 8 of 18 commands.
- **IDK** — information-dense keyword (e.g. "think hard", "model_set heavy").
- **Proof of value** — review-step evidence: numbered screenshots (next: video) posted to the review system.
- **Composable agentic primitives** — the secret; SDLC is one arbitrary arrangement ("a package to deliver a message").
- **YOLO mode / maximum confidence mode** — Dan's names for ZTE's no-review posture ("yellow mode" = yolo mode; "o4 many" = o4-mini; "agent decoding" = agentic coding).

## Bridge to the rest of TAC

- Backward: TAC-4 built PITER and the first ADWs; TAC-5 built the loops ZTE's gates rely on (tests, review, resolution); TAC-6 made agents single-purpose and docs conditional — tac-7 runs all of it in parallel and removes the last human step.
- Forward (51:37–53:20): Lesson 8 revisits "the atoms of agentic engineering" and their compositions across codebase types (web app, CLI, notebooks) — "master them and you can build any molecular structure you need" — plus positioning for today's and tomorrow's engineering. Closing question of this lesson: run away, stand still, move toward, or sprint?

1	# TAC-7 — Outdated vs Current (course era → mid-2026)
2	
3	TAC-7 ages unusually well because its payload is a *North Star and a set of primitives*, not a toolchain: the velocity scale (in-loop → out-loop → ZTE), the presence KPI, and "the secret is composable agentic primitives, not the SDLC" are timeless, and Dan pre-empts the churn on camera ("I don't care how you scale up your agent environments, it only matters that you can"). But it's the Advanced, second-to-last lesson, wired to a specific mid-2025 tooling moment, and six things have moved. For each: what the course shows, what current practice is, and whether the book needs an overlay. Every gap below narrows the *plumbing*; none touches the doctrine.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## 1. Hand-rolled worktree orchestration → isolation as a first-class platform feature  ⟵ the big named gap
8	
9	**Course era:** parallel isolation is built from raw materials — `git worktree add -b` from `origin/main`, base-36-hash port arithmetic (9100–9114 / 9200–9214), an agent-run `/install_worktree` prompt, and `scripts/purge_tree.sh` to reclaim the full-repo copies. Pedagogically perfect: every moving part is visible.
10	**Current:** Claude Code (mid-2026) exposes the same tactic natively — worktree-isolated subagents/tasks, sandboxed bash, and cloud/remote agent execution; multi-agent fan-out over isolated environments is a standard orchestration pattern rather than custom scripting. The CONCEPT — isolated, parallel, disposable agent environments with per-run state — transfers unchanged; the code you'd write today is smaller.
11	**Book treatment:** overlay REQUIRED. Teach the hand-rolled worktree version first (you see the ports, the state, the install), then show the same isolation as native worktree-isolated agents.
12	**Overlay:** `fop_yxV-mPo` — *Codebase Singularity* (include_in_phase1: **yes**) — TAC-7 is the lesson where "the codebase runs itself" stops being a vision and becomes a demo; this video develops that self-operating end-state. (Deferred out of TAC-1 explicitly *to* this lesson.)
13	
14	## 2. `subprocess claude -p` pipelines → the Claude Agent SDK
15	
16	**Course era:** `adws/adw_modules/agent.py` is a subprocess wrapper — `claude -p --model X --output-format stream-json --verbose --dangerously-skip-permissions`, JSONL parsing, a `[1,3,5]s` retry ladder, per-agent session capture.
17	**Current:** that layer is exactly what the Claude Agent SDK (Python/TS) now provides first-class — structured outputs, hooks, session management, and error semantics. The ADW architecture maps 1:1; a 2026 rebuild swaps `agent.py` for the SDK and keeps every workflow script's shape.
18	**Book treatment:** margin note on the `agent.py` walkthrough — "this is the SDK, hand-rolled"; teach the ADW composition idea as durable, the subprocess plumbing as period detail.
19	**Overlay:** `6fCqj4xFCZI` — *How Claude Code CHANGED Engineering Forever* (include_in_phase1: **yes**) — bridges the ADW plumbing the student just read to how the same embedding is done today.
20	
21	## 3. Reusable engineering as `.claude/commands` prompt files → Agent Skills
22	
23	**Course era:** engineering is templated into 33 command prompts discovered by convention, plus the `conditional_docs.md` routing table — which is essentially hand-rolled skill discovery / progressive disclosure ("this lets our agents scale with the size of our codebase").
24	**Current:** Agent Skills (`SKILL.md` with frontmatter, on-demand loading, composability) are the first-class packaging for the same idea; the conditional-docs pattern is precisely what Skills' progressive disclosure does natively.
25	**Book treatment:** overlay for the "template your engineering" section; teach the committed-prompt encoding, then show its current form as a Skill.
26	**Overlay:** `X2ciJedw2vU` — *RAW Agentic Coding: ZERO to Agent SKILL* (include_in_phase1: **yes**) — the committed one-purpose prompt becomes a `SKILL.md`.
27	
28	## 4. Model names and model-set economics are period detail
29	
30	**Course era:** `SLASH_COMMAND_MODEL_MAP` hardcodes `sonnet` / `opus` aliases circa mid-2025, and the demo app bumps `gpt-4.1` → `o4-mini` as its worked chore.
31	**Current:** model families have turned over since (Claude 4-class → Claude 5 era); the specific ids are dated the day they ship. The durable idea is the **base/heavy KNOB** — per-command compute allocation via an IDK stored in state — not any model name. Update the map's *values*, keep its *shape*.
32	**Book treatment:** "period detail" callout on the model-map frame (t1010); teach the knob and the 8-of-18 selectivity as the transferable lesson.
33	**Overlay:** none required.
34	
35	## 5. ZTE guardrails have matured beyond an uppercase check
36	
37	**Course era:** the auto-merge safety is charming prompt-level engineering — `/classify_adw` refuses `adw_sdlc_ZTE_iso` unless "ZTE" is literally uppercase — plus the pipeline's own gates (test/review abort, 8-field state validation, three-way worktree check, `--no-ff` merge with branch-restore).
38	**Current:** production practice layers *deterministic* controls around auto-merge: branch protection + required CI checks, permission modes and hooks gating tool use, environment-scoped credentials, staged deploys / canaries, and merge queues. Dan hints at exactly this evolution in-lesson — "add that key deploy check step, a bunch of deterministic deploy checks... parallelize the review step so three agents have to agree — run the fusion chain on agents."
39	**Book treatment:** teach the in-repo gates as the *concept* (a pipeline that refuses to merge in N places), then a "current practice" callout naming the deterministic controls a real deploy would add. Keep the uppercase interlock as a teaching artifact of prompt-level safety, not a recommendation.
40	**Overlay:** none required (Dan's own "deterministic deploy checks / three-agent fusion" line carries it).
41	
42	## 6. Review evidence: screenshots → video and richer review products
43	
44	**Course era:** the review step's proof is 1–5 numbered screenshots uploaded to R2 and posted to the issue.
45	**Current:** the lesson names its own next step — "the next most obvious one to build out is video. Have your agents take video, upload it to a cloud bucket, and post the URLs." The repo's `playwright-mcp-config.json` *already records* 1920×1080 video per run, and Dan calls comprehensive review systems "an entire product category that is important to build out" — which is precisely what agent-review tooling became.
46	**Book treatment:** footnote the video path as the intended evolution (the config is already there — see lab stretch S7); keep screenshots as the worked example. The principle — proof lands IN the review system, zero clicks to verify — transfers unchanged.
47	**Overlay:** none required.
48	
49	---
50	
51	## What has NOT aged (teach with full confidence)
52	
53	- The **Agentic Engineering Velocity Scale** — in-loop → out-loop → ZTE — and that it's a per-problem-class gradient, not a switch.
54	- **Presence** as the KPI under the whole course arc: TAC-1 removed typing, TAC-7 removes reviewing, presence tracks both.
55	- **The secret: composable agentic primitives**, with the SDLC demoted to one arbitrary arrangement ("a package to deliver a message"). This is the course's thesis and has no expiry.
56	- **Review = proof of value** ("is what we built what we asked for?", proved), distinct from testing; blockers-only resolution.
57	- The **ADW state object** as pipeline memory outside the context window — the thing that lets single-purpose agents chain.
58	- **Isolation, parallelism, disposability** as the requirement (worktrees are one implementation of it).
59	- The **base/heavy compute knob** — encode the allocation once, invoke with one word.
60	- **Evidence-gated, per-class** decisions to drop review — KPIs, not vibes; "how else will you know unless you're trying?"
61	- **"Target" ZTE**: chores → bugs → features; a North Star you earn, not a day-one state.
62	- The **belief section** — "if you don't believe your agents can run your codebase, you're cooked"; "prepared to win, not right."
63	- **Verify countable claims against source, not docs** — the README-says-squash / code-does-`--no-ff` drift is a permanent teaching artifact, not a dated feature.
64

68	|---|---|---|---|
69	| 1 | `fop_yxV-mPo` — Codebase Singularity | operationalizes tactic (the self-operating codebase this lesson demos) | ✅ |
70	| 2 | `6fCqj4xFCZI` — How Claude Code CHANGED Engineering Forever | named hole (`agent.py` subprocess → Agent SDK) | ✅ |
71	| 3 | `X2ciJedw2vU` — RAW Agentic Coding: ZERO to Agent SKILL | corrects outdated (command prompts / conditional_docs → Skills) | ✅ |
72	| 4 | `hGg3nWp7afg` — 3 Codebase Folders | ai_docs/specs/app_docs get only passing reference here | ❌ defer to the context lessons / volume map |

# TAC-7 — Outdated vs Current (course era → mid-2026)

TAC-7 ages unusually well because its payload is a *North Star and a set of primitives*, not a toolchain: the velocity scale (in-loop → out-loop → ZTE), the presence KPI, and "the secret is composable agentic primitives, not the SDLC" are timeless, and Dan pre-empts the churn on camera ("I don't care how you scale up your agent environments, it only matters that you can"). But it's the Advanced, second-to-last lesson, wired to a specific mid-2025 tooling moment, and six things have moved. For each: what the course shows, what current practice is, and whether the book needs an overlay. Every gap below narrows the *plumbing*; none touches the doctrine.

---

## 1. Hand-rolled worktree orchestration → isolation as a first-class platform feature  ⟵ the big named gap

**Course era:** parallel isolation is built from raw materials — `git worktree add -b` from `origin/main`, base-36-hash port arithmetic (9100–9114 / 9200–9214), an agent-run `/install_worktree` prompt, and `scripts/purge_tree.sh` to reclaim the full-repo copies. Pedagogically perfect: every moving part is visible.
**Current:** Claude Code (mid-2026) exposes the same tactic natively — worktree-isolated subagents/tasks, sandboxed bash, and cloud/remote agent execution; multi-agent fan-out over isolated environments is a standard orchestration pattern rather than custom scripting. The CONCEPT — isolated, parallel, disposable agent environments with per-run state — transfers unchanged; the code you'd write today is smaller.
**Book treatment:** overlay REQUIRED. Teach the hand-rolled worktree version first (you see the ports, the state, the install), then show the same isolation as native worktree-isolated agents.
**Overlay:** `fop_yxV-mPo` — *Codebase Singularity* (include_in_phase1: **yes**) — TAC-7 is the lesson where "the codebase runs itself" stops being a vision and becomes a demo; this video develops that self-operating end-state. (Deferred out of TAC-1 explicitly *to* this lesson.)

## 2. `subprocess claude -p` pipelines → the Claude Agent SDK

**Course era:** `adws/adw_modules/agent.py` is a subprocess wrapper — `claude -p --model X --output-format stream-json --verbose --dangerously-skip-permissions`, JSONL parsing, a `[1,3,5]s` retry ladder, per-agent session capture.
**Current:** that layer is exactly what the Claude Agent SDK (Python/TS) now provides first-class — structured outputs, hooks, session management, and error semantics. The ADW architecture maps 1:1; a 2026 rebuild swaps `agent.py` for the SDK and keeps every workflow script's shape.
**Book treatment:** margin note on the `agent.py` walkthrough — "this is the SDK, hand-rolled"; teach the ADW composition idea as durable, the subprocess plumbing as period detail.
**Overlay:** `6fCqj4xFCZI` — *How Claude Code CHANGED Engineering Forever* (include_in_phase1: **yes**) — bridges the ADW plumbing the student just read to how the same embedding is done today.

## 3. Reusable engineering as `.claude/commands` prompt files → Agent Skills

**Course era:** engineering is templated into 33 command prompts discovered by convention, plus the `conditional_docs.md` routing table — which is essentially hand-rolled skill discovery / progressive disclosure ("this lets our agents scale with the size of our codebase").
**Current:** Agent Skills (`SKILL.md` with frontmatter, on-demand loading, composability) are the first-class packaging for the same idea; the conditional-docs pattern is precisely what Skills' progressive disclosure does natively.
**Book treatment:** overlay for the "template your engineering" section; teach the committed-prompt encoding, then show its current form as a Skill.
**Overlay:** `X2ciJedw2vU` — *RAW Agentic Coding: ZERO to Agent SKILL* (include_in_phase1: **yes**) — the committed one-purpose prompt becomes a `SKILL.md`.

## 4. Model names and model-set economics are period detail

**Course era:** `SLASH_COMMAND_MODEL_MAP` hardcodes `sonnet` / `opus` aliases circa mid-2025, and the demo app bumps `gpt-4.1` → `o4-mini` as its worked chore.
**Current:** model families have turned over since (Claude 4-class → Claude 5 era); the specific ids are dated the day they ship. The durable idea is the **base/heavy KNOB** — per-command compute allocation via an IDK stored in state — not any model name. Update the map's *values*, keep its *shape*.
**Book treatment:** "period detail" callout on the model-map frame (t1010); teach the knob and the 8-of-18 selectivity as the transferable lesson.
**Overlay:** none required.

## 5. ZTE guardrails have matured beyond an uppercase check

**Course era:** the auto-merge safety is charming prompt-level engineering — `/classify_adw` refuses `adw_sdlc_ZTE_iso` unless "ZTE" is literally uppercase — plus the pipeline's own gates (test/review abort, 8-field state validation, three-way worktree check, `--no-ff` merge with branch-restore).
**Current:** production practice layers *deterministic* controls around auto-merge: branch protection + required CI checks, permission modes and hooks gating tool use, environment-scoped credentials, staged deploys / canaries, and merge queues. Dan hints at exactly this evolution in-lesson — "add that key deploy check step, a bunch of deterministic deploy checks... parallelize the review step so three agents have to agree — run the fusion chain on agents."
**Book treatment:** teach the in-repo gates as the *concept* (a pipeline that refuses to merge in N places), then a "current practice" callout naming the deterministic controls a real deploy would add. Keep the uppercase interlock as a teaching artifact of prompt-level safety, not a recommendation.
**Overlay:** none required (Dan's own "deterministic deploy checks / three-agent fusion" line carries it).

## 6. Review evidence: screenshots → video and richer review products

**Course era:** the review step's proof is 1–5 numbered screenshots uploaded to R2 and posted to the issue.
**Current:** the lesson names its own next step — "the next most obvious one to build out is video. Have your agents take video, upload it to a cloud bucket, and post the URLs." The repo's `playwright-mcp-config.json` *already records* 1920×1080 video per run, and Dan calls comprehensive review systems "an entire product category that is important to build out" — which is precisely what agent-review tooling became.
**Book treatment:** footnote the video path as the intended evolution (the config is already there — see lab stretch S7); keep screenshots as the worked example. The principle — proof lands IN the review system, zero clicks to verify — transfers unchanged.
**Overlay:** none required.

---

## What has NOT aged (teach with full confidence)

- The **Agentic Engineering Velocity Scale** — in-loop → out-loop → ZTE — and that it's a per-problem-class gradient, not a switch.
- **Presence** as the KPI under the whole course arc: TAC-1 removed typing, TAC-7 removes reviewing, presence tracks both.
- **The secret: composable agentic primitives**, with the SDLC demoted to one arbitrary arrangement ("a package to deliver a message"). This is the course's thesis and has no expiry.
- **Review = proof of value** ("is what we built what we asked for?", proved), distinct from testing; blockers-only resolution.
- The **ADW state object** as pipeline memory outside the context window — the thing that lets single-purpose agents chain.
- **Isolation, parallelism, disposability** as the requirement (worktrees are one implementation of it).
- The **base/heavy compute knob** — encode the allocation once, invoke with one word.
- **Evidence-gated, per-class** decisions to drop review — KPIs, not vibes; "how else will you know unless you're trying?"
- **"Target" ZTE**: chores → bugs → features; a North Star you earn, not a day-one state.
- The **belief section** — "if you don't believe your agents can run your codebase, you're cooked"; "prepared to win, not right."
- **Verify countable claims against source, not docs** — the README-says-squash / code-does-`--no-ff` drift is a permanent teaching artifact, not a dated feature.

## Phase-1 overlay decision (strict, per brief: max 1–3)

| # | Video | Maps to | Include |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `fop_yxV-mPo` — Codebase Singularity | operationalizes tactic (the self-operating codebase this lesson demos) | ✅ |
| 2 | `6fCqj4xFCZI` — How Claude Code CHANGED Engineering Forever | named hole (`agent.py` subprocess → Agent SDK) | ✅ |
| 3 | `X2ciJedw2vU` — RAW Agentic Coding: ZERO to Agent SKILL | corrects outdated (command prompts / conditional_docs → Skills) | ✅ |
| 4 | `hGg3nWp7afg` — 3 Codebase Folders | ai_docs/specs/app_docs get only passing reference here | ❌ defer to the context lessons / volume map |

Exactly **3** included (within the 1–3 cap), matching `extract.json`'s `yt_overlay_candidates`. TAC-7 uses all three because its three biggest plumbing gaps (worktree orchestration, subprocess pipelines, prompt-file packaging) each have a clean, on-topic current-practice video.

*Caveat: IDs/titles come from the orchestration seed pool (oembed-verified in the TAC-1 cross-review — `fop_yxV-mPo`, `6fCqj4xFCZI`, `X2ciJedw2vU`); re-verify each resolves and its content matches its title before publishing overlay links — no video fetching was performed in this extract pass, per brief.*
